title: Council Post: HR Leaders Must Have A Clear Strategy For AI Adoption
text:
Anne Krog Iversen is the Co-founder, Chief DNA & Culture Officer at TimeXtender.
As artificial intelligence continues to advance at an unprecedented pace, it's becoming increasingly clear that the future of work is undergoing a seismic shift. The integration of AI into various industries and workplaces is no longer a distant possibility but a reality that we must embrace and navigate with care.
This technological revolution is particularly transformative for the field of human resources. AI is rapidly being adopted to streamline and augment processes like recruitment, performance management, talent development and workforce planning. While these advancements offer immense potential to enhance HR teams' efficiency and decision-making, the increasing prevalence also raises valid concerns about data quality, bias and ethical implications.
Data Quality's Impact On Crucial HR Functions
As AI systems become more deeply integrated into your HR systems, algorithms will have a far-reaching impact on your ability to build a diverse, engaged and high-performing workforce. But these tools are only as good as the data they're trained on, and if that data is flawed or biased, the outcomes can be detrimental to your organization's most valuable asset: its people. Here are three key areas that data quality affects.
• Hiring And Recruitment: If the AI system you adopt is trained on historical hiring data that reflects biases against certain demographics, it may systematically overlook qualified candidates from underrepresented groups. This could hinder efforts to build a diverse and inclusive workforce, depriving your company of top talent and even exposing it to legal risks.
• Performance Management: Inaccurate or biased performance data fed into algorithm-driven systems could result in unfair evaluations and compensation decisions. This could demotivate employees, increase turnover and erode trust in your organization's commitment to meritocracy.
• Talent Development: Low-quality data can fail to identify high-potential employees for growth opportunities or recommend training programs that don't match employees' needs. Poor development processes stunt employee growth, hinder succession planning efforts and limit your ability to develop a future-ready workforce.
Failing to address or be aware of these issues could undermine your HR team's core function of building an engaged, high-performing and inclusive workforce. You should take proactive steps to audit and curate training data, such as identifying and removing discriminatory variables, increasing representation of underrepresented groups and incorporating human oversight to catch errors or unintended consequences.
3 Considerations Before AI Implementation
If you're looking to add AI technology to any of your HR processes, you should think deeply about several key factors. Here are three considerations to make as you approach AI adoption.
1. Potential Biases In AI Training Data: Avoiding biases in your AI systems is vital. Be sure to audit data sources, find any biases and implement strategies to remove discriminatory variables or increase the representation of any missing groups.
2. Transparent Decision-Making Processes: Any algorithm-driven HR processes must be designed with transparency and ease of understanding in mind. All employees, even those who won't use the systems in question, should understand how decisions or recommendations are made.
3. Impact On The Workforce And Existing Processes: You'll need AI technology that best fits your use case and documentation needs. So you must first assess how introducing a new system will affect job roles, workflows and processes within your organization. Then, you should develop strategies for workforce retraining, ethical AI training and facilitated AI dialogues based on that assessment.
With these factors top of mind, you can approach AI implementation in a responsible, ethical and well-informed manner. This will help you ensure the benefits of new technologies are realized while mitigating potential risks and negative impacts on the workforce and organizational processes.
AI Can Enhance Your Organization's Community Impact
As the world grapples with pressing environmental challenges and the need for more socially responsible business practices, AI can be a powerful tool to drive positive change. By harnessing its capabilities ethically, you can help ensure your organization is actively contributing to the well-being of local communities and the planet as a whole.
Enabling AI-powered sustainable practices can optimize resource usage and reduce waste across supply chains, manufacturing processes and logistics operations. This minimizes your organization's environmental footprint.
You can also foster better community engagement with certain AI technologies. Generative tools allow for personalized communications and content that engages community members effectively. For example, your organization could highlight its commitment to relevant environmental and social issues.
By leveraging AI, you can drive operational efficiencies, innovate sustainable solutions, enhance environmental stewardship and build stronger connections with local communities. This is an effective strategy to help pave the way for a more sustainable, equitable future.
In Summary
As organizations navigate the future of work, it's crucial that HR leaders understand how to approach AI technology with intentionality and ethical considerations. While it offers immense potential for enhancing productivity, driving innovation and creating a more sustainable future, you must remain vigilant about its limitations and inherent biases. By thoughtfully integrating AI, your organization can unlock new levels of efficiency and creativity while prioritizing ethical decision-making and community well-being. Ultimately, responsible and equitable adoption will provide a path forward that empowers both organizations and individuals to thrive.

title: Council Post: Five Lessons From 20 Years Of Developing And Deploying AI
text:
João Graça is the cofounder and CTO of Unbabel.
This year marks two decades since I began my career in what is now commonly known as "AI"—natural language processing. Here are some of the major lessons learned in that time, as both a research scientist and being responsible for building commercial products.
Lesson 1: Be Pragmatic—Leverage What Exists And Build Around That
In 2013, I cofounded Unbabel with the idea of becoming “the world’s translation layer,” combining AI and human effort to solve multilingual translation at scale. By sending machine-translation (MT) chunks to bilingual individuals for approval or amendment via a mobile interface, we aimed to achieve higher-quality translation at a lower cost and greater speed than either pure human translation or pure MT.
To accomplish this, we needed access to the inner workings of the translation model, which no third-party provider like Google or Microsoft would grant. So we built our own MT model based on the open-source Moses Statistical MT library, which I had contributed to during my Ph.D. It wasn’t as advanced as Google’s, but it was ours!
Eventually, we developed our own library from scratch, but Moses enabled us to move from idea to proof of concept to validation with our first customers—and helped us become the first Portuguese company accepted into Y Combinator (winter 2013).
So, the first lesson is to be pragmatic: Leverage existing resources and build around them. Focus on proving product-market fit quickly and only develop proprietary AI when it’s a core part of your offering. There are many free tools and resources available today, so make good use of them and differentiate from there.
Lesson 2: Partner With Academia To Augment Your Capabilities
After Y Combinator, we needed to move beyond prototypes and build scalable solutions. We built dozens of models for different language pairs and customers but needed to solve many research challenges to stay ahead.
Lacking bandwidth, we decided to partner with universities conducting relevant research, proposing big, hairy, audacious challenges that would interest top post-grad students—and solving our real customer problems.
It was a win-win-win—for the students, the universities and us—and allowed us to scale our research team by co-advising masters and Ph.D. theses. This then led to bigger research projects, creating a flywheel effect resulting in dozens of papers and product innovations that have kept us in business ever since.
The lesson here is to partner with academia to augment your capabilities. It’s a mutually beneficial arrangement that fosters success.
Lesson 3: Your AI Is Only As Good As What Customers Can Use
Our growing research team developed cutting-edge research, publishing at top conferences, but these outputs were not benefiting customers as intended due to a gap between product engineering and research teams. Mismatched priorities, working methods, tooling and incentives were the main issues.
Our first approach was to integrate researchers into cross-functional product teams, but this pressured them to focus on short-term goals, losing long-term focus. We then split them into AI research and applied AI teams, but conflicting priorities, non-production-ready research code and differing infrastructure and datasets persisted.
We have since closed most of the gap with shared roadmaps, datasets, codebases, benchmarks, hardware infrastructure and aligned incentives. In fact, the success metric for our research team is the percentage of words translated in production by their models, allowing product teams to deliver the best quality for customers.
As Charlie Munger once said, “Show me the incentives, and I will show you the outcome.”
Lesson 4: Align AI Research With Business Needs
Unbabel was initially focused on translating millions of customer service emails. As our MT engines improved, we realized we didn’t always need a human in the loop, but we needed a way to determine when.
Quality estimation (QE) research, which predicts the work needed to bring a machine-translated text to human quality, was an emerging field of research and suited our needs perfectly.
We formed a QE team and trained models using our historical data. This surpassed expectations and quickly became the best QE system worldwide for the past eight years, according to the yearly World Machine Translation shared task competition.
The lesson here is to align business needs with research opportunities. If you find this intersection, you will uncover state-of-the-art value and stay ahead.
Lesson 5: You Can Always Differentiate From The Tech Giants
Once ChatGPT came out, the biggest question I had to answer was what would happen to Unbabel. “Can’t you do it all with an LLM and prompting?”
The question makes me smile because it is not much different from the question we were asked in 2013 when we started the company: “Hasn’t Google Translate already solved this problem?”
The answer to both is no. Building production systems to solve specific customer problems involves much more than is immediately apparent. Over more than a decade, I’ve realized you can differentiate from tech giants in three ways.
1. Cost: State-of-the-art models quickly become commodified. You can leverage these for free and focus on specialized, profitable value creation atop them.
2. Quality: By focusing on specific use cases and customer data sets, you can fine-tune models to a degree no one else can. Proprietary data and models provide higher quality than generalist platforms.
3. Privacy And Security: Plenty of companies are not interested in signing over their most sensitive data to the tech giants. If you can protect your customers’ data and help them leverage its full value, then you will be able to build an incredibly successful business.
For all the talk of “no moats in AI,” these are significant differentiators for building a leading global business.

title: Council Post: How Marketers Can Unlock AI For Growth: Four Essential Strategies
text:
Santhi Suryanarayanan Ramesh is Global C-Suite Executive, Board Advisor, and named one of Forbes Most Influential CMOs in 2022.
Today, AI is a mandatory technological capability to remain competitive. In fact, according to a BCG survey, 85% of CEOs identified AI as a strategic priority for investment to drive the next business transformation.
Making AI a priority presents a unique opportunity for marketers, provided that they understand how to harness its power to accelerate growth. In this article, I'll examine four strategies that can help marketing leaders capitalize on AI with speed and agility to stay ahead of the next wave of digital transformation.
Future-Forward Decisioning
According to the World Economic Forum, the effective use of AI in strategic decision-making will be one of the biggest determinants of future competitiveness. Along with the more commonly understood generative AI, AI also offers predictive models that can connect diverse qualitative and quantitative data points to predict futuristic scenarios and recommend solutions.
Marketers can leverage these predictive analytical tools to fast-track business analysis and enable decisions swiftly across the product and marketing life cycle. For instance, I've seen marketers use these tools to:
1. Unearth consumer needs that could present a white space opportunity or pinpoint the next trend in product development.
2. Guide strategic portfolio decisions including SKU rationalization, item expansion and pricing strategies.
An important factor to keep in mind, though, is that most predictive models analyze historical data. It is critical to include futuristic macro-outlook, outyear growth projections and consumer-need evolutions over time in the analysis, though these insights can be challenging to obtain.
Agile Personalization At Scale
Today, with the diversity of consumer segments and different consumer personas within each segment, personalized messaging is key to driving engagement and conversion.
However, one-to-one marketing is time-consuming and complex. AI enables marketers to be more efficient and effective in reaching consumers across the marketing funnel. Specifically, AI can be deployed to:
1. Identify the most profitable consumer cohort for the brand and message consumers with the appropriate message at the best touchpoint at the right time.
2. Deliver immersive experiences to consumers that enhance engagement and affinity with the brand in a seamless omnichannel manner.
Marketers will need first-party data to engage with consumers on a one-to-one basis. Leaders who can bridge a variety of data sources and access data across marketing channels will be the most likely to succeed with personalization efforts.
Marketing Operational Efficiency
According to an April 2024 survey by EY, many CEOs are prioritizing investments in AI to boost productivity.
AI, for example, can increase the efficiency of day-to-day marketing operations. AI bots and machine learning models can be built to automate repetitive tasks in marketing operations so that marketers can focus their time and energy on strategic thinking. Areas that can benefit greatly from automation using AI include:
1. Improving content optimization efforts and search bidding investments to ensure that products are more visible on the digital shelf.
2. Speeding up content creation by leveraging master brand content, personalizing for the touchpoint and adapting for the target consumer.
Marketing leaders should be aware, though, that every automation effort comes with errors. It is also common for content created by AI to lack personality. To counter these concerns, every automated process should include checks and balances with human intervention to ensure that the content is relevant and maintains the brand tone and voice.
Enhanced Customer Service
AI tools like chatbots and virtual assistants have helped companies find the always-important balance between lowering operational costs, increasing customer satisfaction and maintaining employee morale. As McKinsey pointed out in their case study of an Asian bank, companies can best leverage these tools by focusing on the future of service and rethinking every customer touchpoint.
For instance, companies are already using AI to improve customer service by:
1. Analyzing customer interactions and then providing personalized suggestions and marketing messages.
2. Using voice and image recognition interfaces to simplify user experiences and enable intuitive natural interactions.
As with all AI solutions, data is crucial here. To provide superior customer service, ensure that chatbots and intelligent systems are trained on enough data to be versatile in their recognition of phrases and in answering questions. In addition, any customer-facing technology should function in multiple languages and be able to communicate appropriately with multilingual audiences.
Conclusion
Marketers can unleash the power of AI to drive transformational growth. Leaders can make better decisions, drive operational efficiency, increase engagement and enhance customer service by applying AI throughout the marketing life cycle.
At the same time, overcoming challenges in data availability, privacy and managing ethical dilemmas will be critical to success. Leaders who build an ecosystem of partners to test, learn and scale AI-based technological capabilities will have the best chance of winning with AI.
The possibilities are endless for those who are willing to experiment and take the leap now to propel growth with AI.

title: Council Post: Can AI Be Leveraged In A More Sustainable Way?
text:
Russ Kennedy is Chief Product Officer at Nasuni.
The evidence for AI's energy appetite is mounting quickly. Advanced AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude depend on the compute capacity of vast data centers, and the graphics processing units (GPUs) required to run these models demand anywhere from four times to 15 times more than the traditional CPUs that do most of the computational work inside. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), a Google search that makes full use of AI, including an LLM-powered summary of scanned pages, consumes 10 times as much energy as a traditional query.
Training the foundational models behind the latest AI tools is becoming increasingly energy-intensive, expanding by four to five times per year. It's no surprise, then, that the IEA estimates the electricity consumption of global data centers could double by 2026.
We can't continue on this path—especially not on a planet suffering from intense heat, droughts and extreme weather events due to anthropogenic climate change.
The hyperscalers have set ambitious goals to reduce their reliance on traditional fuel-powered electricity and fresh water used to cool data centers. But these sustainability efforts have veered off track due in part to the increased focus on energy-intensive AI and the rapid expansion of data centers to meet demand for cloud services. Amazon reports that they have met their energy-neutral impact goals, but Google and Microsoft both admitted to a spike in emissions in their latest sustainability reports.
As technologists and users, we have to do better, and I believe we will, but we need to realign our priorities and strategies. Here are five possible ways to do that.
Deploy advanced AI tactically.
If an inch of snow falls on my front steps in the winter, I grab a shovel, not a snowblower. Similarly, we don’t need to deploy fantastically advanced AI engines for every task. The Gemini-powered summaries that appear at the top of some Google searches are a good example of selective application.
If I search for something simple and specific, then some old-fashioned links to pages turn up. But if I broaden my query, an AI summary generated from a list of relevant pages appears at the top. Even here, however, the use of an energy-intensive large language model is questionable. I wonder whether this level of intelligence is necessary, given how effectively standard search has functioned for years.
Develop smaller models.
Typically, I write and revise my columns in Microsoft Word. This program has certainly advanced over the years, but its computational demands have grown as well. The first version of MS Word, released for Windows back in 1990, required 640K of RAM. Today, PC manufacturers suggest having more than 4GB of RAM available. Yes, the modern version is better, but is it 6,400 times better?
We can’t let enterprise AI models follow the same path. The next generation of tools should not only be applied tactfully but designed with energy efficiency in mind. Context window size and performance benchmarks should not be the only measures of progress. We need smaller, more efficient language models that are sized appropriately for specific tasks and use only the compute needed to generate impactful results.
Advance sustainable computing.
This should come as no surprise, but AI itself can help rebalance this energy deficit if put to good use. Researchers and companies could use AI to reduce losses as electricity is distributed throughout the power grid, uncover new and more sustainable materials for use in data centers or develop more energy-efficient chips.
Google claims that one of its new chips is 67% more energy efficient than previous models and that they have identified changes in their processes that can reduce the energy required to train a model by 100 times. This is the kind of work we need to continue.
Explore novel renewables.
As the industry’s energy demands grow, we may need to look beyond wind and solar to meet our expected demand with alternative sources of green power, including geothermal and nuclear. The latter is a controversial technology for good reason, but the industry has also been designing plants the same way for many decades. Small modular reactors may be a potential solution, along with novel approaches like the Bill-Gates-funded startup TerraPower, which aims to have a smaller, safer nuclear plant operational in Wyoming by 2030.
Sharpen regulations and oversight.
Given the challenges the world faces around climate change, a technology that demands so much energy and water should be regulated. We should not leave it up to companies to decide how much electricity and freshwater they consume—not when these are both limited resources. There must be reasonable boundaries and controls that balance the energy needs of hyperscalers with those of the surrounding communities and countries that host their data centers.
The fear of AI typically centers around superintelligent machines developing their own goals. While the timeline associated with this potential threat is uncertain, the risk of AI’s thirst for electricity is imminent, and we can’t bury our heads in the proverbial sand.
We can’t simply marvel in wonder at the capabilities of these models without judging them by their impact on the grid. AI’s electricity problem is happening now, and as enterprise leaders, we need to address it now before it gets worse.

title: How Generative AI Helps Predictive AI
text:
Not all business problems are best addressed with generative AI. For some, prediction is the solution.
Take misinformation detection. Imagine you run a social media platform and, for certain high-risk channels, a third of user posts convey misinformation. As a result, your business is getting slammed in the press.
As with fighting fraud, managing credit risk and targeting marketing, this is exactly the kind of problem that demands prediction. On the one hand, you can't trust a machine to filter every post automatically. On the other, you can't have every post manually reviewed—that's too expensive.
Enter predictive AI, which flags (predicts) cases of interest. For misinformation detection, this means flagging the posts most likely to convey misinformation, which in turn should be audited by humans and potentially blocked.
A single chart summarizes the value of doing so:
This plots the money saved (vertical axis) against the portion of posts manually audited (horizontal axis). The leftmost position corresponds with auditing zero posts, which would mean no misinformation is blocked, and the rightmost position corresponds with auditing all posts, which could mean all misinformation is blocked, but would cost a lot of human labor.
The shape of this curve guides you to balance between auditing too few and too many. In this case, you would save the most by auditing the top 51% most likely to be fraudulent. That's where you'd maximize the reduction in cost—in comparison to not auditing any posts and not blocking any misinformation.
These savings are estimated in part based on two different kinds of cost:
1) The cost to manually audit a post (set at $4 for this example).
2) The cost of misinformation going undetected (set at $10 for this example).
While the first of these two can be objectively established based on the cost of labor, the second is subjective, so there may be no definitive way to determine its setting. Many use cases of predictive AI face a similar dilemma. How do you put a number on the cost of a medical condition going undetected? Or the cost of an important email message being incorrectly relegated to your spam folder? For all such projects, it's vital that stakeholders be given the capability to vary the cost setting so that they can see how it affects the shape of this curve. That is the topic of a follow-up article that I'll publish soon.
The peak estimated savings comes to $442,000, based also on an assumed population of 200,000 posts (within the high-risk channels). This means that, if there are 200,000 posts each week, the right setting stands to save the company $442,000 per week.
Most predictive AI projects see a similar effect, where there's a “Goldilocks zone” somewhere in the middle: The value is maximized by not inspecting too many cases, and yet not inspecting too few. After all, that's the value of predictive scores: They prioritize cases so that you can decide where to draw the line—where to set the decision threshold—as to which cases get “treated” (audited, contacted, approved, etc.). The horizontal axis reflects this ordering and the dotted vertical line represents an example setting for the decision threshold.
Yet, most predictive AI projects don’t actually “see” this effect because they don’t go as far as plotting a curve like this. Tracking a business metric like savings is critical, but is not yet common practice. Instead, projects usually only track technical metrics that don’t provide clear insight into the potential business value.
Predicting With A Large Language Model
Predictive models come in all shapes and sizes, including decision trees, logistic regression and ensemble models. But for language-heavy tasks such as misinformation detection, a large language model may be well-suited. Such models usually serve generative AI—to generate draft content—but they can also serve to predict.
To try this out, we tapped a Stanford project that tested various LLMs on various benchmarks, including one that gauges how often a model can establish whether a given statement is true or false. The test cases were designed to evaluate for reading comprehension—they didn't represent the kinds of public misinformation that would more typically appear on social media. So we've used this testbed only to illustrate the mechanics of how an LLM could serve for misinformation detection; this illustration should not be considered a rigorous research project into the effectiveness of this approach.
For each case, OpenAI's GPT-3 (175 billion parameters) was asked multiple times—with some simple, rote variations in the wording—whether the statement was true or false. Each of the LLM's response counted as a “vote” in order to turn these outputs into a predictive score for each test case. Those scores, in turn, are reflected in the chart's ordering, from left to right: Those on the left are predicted as more likely to be false and those on the right as more likely to be true. A bit more than one third, 37%, of the test cases were false statements and the rest true.
No matter which kind of model you use to predict, the value of doing so can usually be represented with a chart like that shown above. The model's utility comes down to that left-to-right ordering. With that valuable prioritization, you then get to choose where to draw the line (the decision threshold).
Beyond the goal of maximizing any one business metric, such as savings or profit, establishing the decision threshold must also take other tradeoffs into consideration. I'll continue with this example in a follow-up article so that we can more holistically navigate the options.

title: In Rare Three-Peat, Andreessen Leads $80 Million AI-Focused Funding Round For Story Protocol
text:
In 2015, Andreessen Horowitz’s Chris Dixon wrote about how PC gaming leveraged online user contributions to drive new revenue. Serial entrepreneur Seung Yoon Lee took this lesson to heart, realizing that the gaming industry's approach to intellectual property (IP)—encouraging experimentation with it, rather than fighting it in court,—was something the newspaper, publishing, and music industries could all learn from. Now, Lee is offering them that opportunity with his “IP blockchain” Story.
Today, PIP Labs, the company behind Story, announced an $80 million Series B raise, led by a16z crypto, with participation from Polychain, Stability AI SVP and board member Scott Trowbridge, K11 founder Adrian Cheng, and digital art collector Cozomo de' Medici. This marks only the second time Andreessen Horowitz's crypto arm has led three funding rounds in a single company—the first being for Coinbase, the largest cryptocurrency trading platform in the U.S.
The Story Protocol facilitates the creation of programmable IP, operating on the premise that intellectual property can be transformed into liquid assets. Jason Zhao, co-founder and chief product officer, who previously led product development at Google’s AI laboratory DeepMind, likens it to “legos”—blocks programmed with metadata that define pricing and any restrictions on use for automated distribution to creators. This creates a positive feedback loop, according to Zhao and Lee, allowing creators to experiment with the confidence that they have permission to use the assets, while IP owners benefit from a share of fees and a steady stream of user-generated ideas. Lee pitches this as a “two-pronged approach”: eliminating the costs of middlemen managing contracts and disputes, while unlocking new revenue streams from fanfiction, remixes, and AI tools that train on their data.
Story was initially built on Ethereum’s test network Sepolia—Ethereum is known for its capacity to host complex applications but also high costs and slow speed,—but PIP Labs is now set to launch its own blockchain on August 27th. This move will give the company greater technical control to implement features like on-chain dispute resolution. Over 200 teams, representing more than 20 million IPs, are preparing to launch on the blockchain, with apps such as Ablo, which allows users to experiment with designs from well-known brands, and Sekai, a platform for storytelling experimentation in comics and anime.
Lee and Zhao aren’t the first to explore blockchain’s potential for IP management. Solana
The technology could fundamentally change how IP is managed, provided it can convince creators, AI developers, gamers, and others to embrace the blockchain rather than bypassing it. Intellectual property infringement happens in a variety of ways, ranging from artificial intelligence companies training their models on news articles without consent to teenagers reimagining beloved book characters on platforms like DeviantArt. Some intentionally skirt the law or navigate gray areas, while others avoid paying or entering agreements simply because they believe it’s unlikely they’ll ever get caught. The volume of IP theft is so large it’s estimated to cost the U.S. economy up to $600 billion annually. For Story to succeed, a broad spectrum of users must choose to secure rights to assets through the blockchain, rather than continuing with the status quo.
Lee is optimistic, drawing parallels to the success of companies like Spotify, which quickly surpassed music pirating sites by attracting over a million U.S. users within its first year. Spotify's ability to convince users that legal alternatives could be more convenient and enjoyable than piracy was key to its rapid adoption. “They did it with insanely great UX [user experience],” Lee says. He is confident that the developers drawn to Story can create applications that make experimenting with IP equally compelling.
“Creators need a modern way to ensure they get compensated for their work. Story takes a proven approach — intellectual property law — and updates it for the age of AI,” wrote Chris Dixon and Carra Wu, partners at Andreessen Horowitz, in a blog post shared with Forbes ahead of the announcement. “[Lee] has consistently impressed us with his combination of big-picture vision and world-class tactical execution.”
Similar to other blockchain initiatives, Story is attracting developers by offering a range of incentives, including grants, marketing support, technical assistance, and fundraising guidance. These resources are provided through the Story Academy, a comprehensive program featuring a 6-7 week accelerator for mid-stage projects and a 12-week incubator for early-stage ventures. The incubator, which began accepting applications in early July and kicks off in September, offers participants $10,000 to $20,000 in initial funding, with the potential to secure up to $50,000 upon reaching key milestones. Meanwhile, those in the Accelerator program can receive an average of $50,000 in grants, with the opportunity to earn up to $100,000. This approach helps explain why Story has raised over $140 million across three funding rounds since May 2023.
The company is also collaborating with legal experts and consultants to provide guidance on crowdfunding, community building, and licensing, including firms like Fenwick, Latham, and Granderson Des Rochers. With their help, the company is developing liquidity and capital formation products for IP owners and studios.
Lee stresses that Story’s mission is to address real-world challenges in IP management, particularly as generative AI creates new urgency for integrating copyright agreements into digital assets. “Everyone is training on other people’s data, and there’s no way for IPs to get compensated,” Lee warns. “If this continues, it will be like ‘Google kills journalism’ times 1000. We want to protect the IP.”

title: Council Post: How AI Will Impact Governance, Risk And Compliance Programs
text:
With 15+ years in the field, Matt serves as VP of Security and CISO at Drata, leading global security, IT, GRC and privacy initiatives.
While the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is still nascent, it is poised to reshape virtually every aspect of our world, and the realm of governance, risk and compliance (GRC) will not escape its influence. AI is already demonstrating its potential to transform how organizations identify and manage risk, maintain compliance and make policy decisions through its ability to process massive datasets, recognize patterns and generate insights. However, its promise is accompanied by new challenges and uncertainties that GRC leaders must contend with.
The Promises Of AI
One of the most significant benefits of AI for GRC decision makers and practitioners is the ability to automate further and augment many compliance processes. By leveraging well-trained models, organizations can more efficiently monitor compliance violations, freeing up human resources for higher-value tasks. AI can also improve risk identification and assessment, sifting through vast amounts of data to spot patterns and anomalies that indicate emerging risks, which, when it comes to third-party risk management, can significantly reduce the amount of time GRC team members spend reviewing hundreds of pages of due diligence artifacts to distill out these key elements. This helps organizations develop readiness plans before events rather than being purely reactive to risk management.
In the due diligence process, AI can enhance both the speed and depth of analysis and can be deployed to automate data collection, document classification and report generation. It can also be used to continuously monitor regulatory changes, gathering and analyzing data that inform changes to the due diligence process. The ability to continually refine the process ensures that it always reflects contemporary needs and remains relevant.
GRC practitioners can use AI-powered natural language processing in several ways. One possibility is the rapid analysis of contracts, security questionnaires, third-party risk management artifacts and other legal documents to surface important clauses, risks and compliance issues. Another is the consumption and synthesis of large volumes of unstructured data, such as news articles and social media posts, to provide a more comprehensive view of potential third-party risks.
While more operational tasks are AI's most prominent use cases, strategic planning and decision making can also be augmented by AI. Its ability to provide predictive insights and perform scenario modeling using large, disparate data sets can yield significant benefits in these activities. By analyzing historical patterns and layering in real-time data from a broad swath of data sources, AI can ultimately help GRC leaders surface and anticipate future risks based on the current state and provide a more robust data set on which to base their decisions and make these risk assessments less subjective and more quantitative.
Risks And Concerns
While AI promises numerous positives in the GRC arena, GRC leaders must address significant concerns before adopting it broadly. One of the most pressing is data privacy and security. The vast amounts of data required to train AI models may contain sensitive data, making both the data sets used to train the models and the models themselves a target for cyberattacks and other exploits specific to AI. Organizations must implement guardrails to protect their AI assets, ensure the privacy and security of the data they use to train their models, protect the use of models used and ensure continuous compliance with recently introduced regulations around the use of AI and existing regulations such as GDPR.
Another primary concern related to AI revolves around ethical issues such as bias, discrimination and a lack of transparency and explainability. In training AI models, garbage in truly equals garbage out. If the training data is biased, the algorithms will perpetuate the biases. The lack of transparency and explainability in AI decision making compounds the problem and can have a harmful impact, especially in sensitive areas like risk scoring and due diligence. To address this, organizations must establish robust AI policies that ensure fairness in the data sets used to train their models and that the AI decision-making process can be easily tracked, understood, validated and corrected if necessary. While we’d ultimately like to get to a point where models can be trusted, many organizations are still encouraged not to rely on outputs from models for key decision-making activities. They will flag prompt outputs as potentially making mistakes.
Because AI promises the benefits of automation and vast simplification, there is a risk of overreliance on AI, leading to complacency and exposing organizations to vulnerabilities and legal liabilities that result from technological failure. Organizations must treat AI as an augmentation mechanism rather than a substitute for human judgment and additional checks to confirm the accuracy of the outputs generated. They should use it to inform and support decision making instead of allowing it to be the sole decision maker. Processes and systems that provide checks and balances that involve human arbitration are essential in ensuring that the unfettered use of AI doesn’t result in damaging consequences.
Organizations must also address the skills gap when implementing AI in their GRC program. This effort will require a significant investment in training, hiring and managing potential workforce displacement as roles become automated. New roles will emerge as companies adapt to the needs of a new paradigm and the demand for talent who knows how to operationalize technology grows. Many security programs include AI assessments as part of their external penetration testing activities to check an organization’s use of AI in their product and encourage their application security team members to increase their knowledge and expertise around AI-related security exploits and weaknesses.
Planning For The Future
While the path forward may still feel nebulous, what is clear is that AI will have a profound and pervasive impact on all facets of life and technology. GRC leaders who can harness the power of AI while navigating its challenges will be well-positioned to steer their organizations toward a more intelligent, risk-aware future. But this requires proactive planning and ongoing vigilance. The costs of AI's risks and uncertainties are too high to leave to chance. The time to start preparing is now.

title: Council Post: Pitfalls All Businesses Should Avoid When Developing An AI Solution
text:
John Schwarz is the Cofounder and Chairman of the Board of Visier, a software analytics provider focused on providing insights into people.
For Microsoft, it was a lesson in how not to train AI.
In 2016, the tech giant released Tay, a chatbot designed to build conversational skills by interacting with people on Twitter. Things soon went sideways, thanks to the data Tay was fed. From its exchanges with a group of Twitter users, the bot quickly learned racist and misogynist language that it spun into a barrage of offensive tweets. Microsoft shut it down within 24 hours.
There’s also a lesson here for companies planning to use the latest generative AI technology to gain insights into their business, whether it’s how much to pay people or which customers are at risk of canceling their subscriptions.
For starters, most companies lack the rich data set an AI model needs to provide accurate and reliable insights specific to their business and industry.
As the cofounder of a company that helps customers gain insights into their HR data, I’ve seen the benefits of having access to the right tools. Here’s why building your own solution is trickier than it might first appear and how the right partner can make a big difference.
When To DIY AI
Let’s say a company wants to develop an AI agent that helps it solve the age-old problem of compensating its employees fairly. Instead of laboriously crunching numbers, wouldn’t it be great if AI could spit out a smart recommendation on everything from salaries to raises and bonuses?
It’s easy enough to license any number of off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs)—from GPT to Gemini, Coral and Falcon—that take questions and provide answers in plain language. Depending on the complexity of the use case, costs might be as little as a few cents a query.
However, for any business that uses AI to inform pay decisions, the model itself is secondary. In this example, what’s important is giving it deep knowledge of compensation in all of its complexity relative to the other people in the team and relative to what is the norm in the industry for a given level of skill and performance.
To gain that knowledge, an AI model needs the proper training. This entails investing in research, feeding it relevant data from within the company and from external sources, and—most importantly—incorporating a human feedback loop to verify and improve results.
This is a primary reason why do-it-yourself AI tools tend to be unreliable. For companies that develop their own solutions, six out of 10 have accuracy issues, one survey found.
Then there’s the expense involved. Although LLMs may cost relatively little, training them to suit a company’s particular needs is a significant effort. For example, Bloomberg reportedly spent many millions developing its LLM. And as always, maintenance is an issue. Every time the LLM base version changes, it must be retrained to provide consistency and reliability.
It’s also worth remembering that most AI projects flop. Their failure rate could be as high as 80%, nearly double that of internal IT projects.
How To Work With An AI Partner
For most companies, a better approach is to find a partner who specializes in developing AI for businesses and has a large data set targeted to their industry and functional needs.
After all, AI is only useful for a business if it’s been trained on relevant data. The more such data you have to train it, the more valuable it gets. In most cases, the only way to obtain enough is to aggregate data from many related businesses.
The compensation example I used above comes from the world of HR and people analytics. Here, access to a critical mass of employee records is essential. When building our own AI assistant for HR, we trained it on tens of millions of records from various industries and locations, representing exceptionally diverse skills.
Importantly, this training uses only metadata, which consists of customers’ queries, not their actual data. The assistant is then “tuned” to each customer to support their unique corporate language. Prompt engineering is essential to prepare it to provide better answers. Finally, it’s important to know what good data actually looks like. A rich source of benchmark data is a key prerequisite.
Partnering with the right vendor means businesses can also ensure their security and privacy needs are met. This means safeguarding confidential data and provisioning access to distinct users in your organization.
For example, a rank-and-file employee asking about compensation for a specific role will only get the company’s desired benchmark relative to the industry, while an authorized manager can see details about individual pay for employees who report to them.
Ultimately, any company planning to harness the power of AI must choose an approach that best suits its needs. In my experience, finding a partner with specialized technology and access to an abundance of relevant industry data gets better results. A company that goes it alone with AI risks creating headaches for itself—and coming up short of the rich, precise insights it needs to drive competitive business outcomes.

title: Council Post: The Competitive Edge: Why Professionals With AI Skills Command Higher Salaries
text:
Michael Beygelman is Executive Vice President of Product at WilsonHCG. He founded Claro Analytics, which was acquired by WilsonHCG in 2022.
In the rapidly evolving industry landscape, a new paradigm is emerging—one where artificial intelligence (AI) is not just a buzzword but a critical skill set commanding premium salaries.
As an industry veteran with nearly three decades of experience in the technology sector and a founder of a labor market intelligence platform, I've witnessed firsthand the transformative power of AI. Today, professionals equipped with AI skills are not just ahead of the curve; they're reshaping the entire tech industry.
The AI Revolution: A $30,000 Salary Differential
The integration of AI has created a stark divide in the job market. Those possessing AI skills are now commanding salaries up to $30,000 more annually than their peers without this expertise, according to our data. This substantial difference underscores a critical message: adapt or risk being left behind.
Recent labor market data paints a vivid picture of the AI revolution. We're seeing a staggering 500% increase in AI-related job postings across both the U.S. and U.K. markets. This surge isn't confined to traditional tech companies; it's permeating all sectors, from finance and healthcare to manufacturing.
Organizations are actively seeking professionals who can harness AI tools to streamline processes, boost efficiency and drive data-informed decision making.
Bridging The AI Skills Gap: A Competitive Advantage
Despite the soaring demand, a significant skills gap persists in the tech industry. Many professionals lack the expertise to effectively utilize advanced AI tools. This gap presents a golden opportunity for those willing to invest in developing these skills.
People with AI proficiency are better positioned to develop innovative solutions that leverage machine learning and deep learning, analyze complex datasets to uncover actionable insights across various business domains and contribute more meaningfully to high-level strategic decisions in their organizations.
It's crucial to understand that AI isn't replacing tech functions—it's elevating them. By leveraging AI for data analysis, automation and predictive modeling, professionals with AI skills can provide valuable insights that drive business decisions. This shift represents a move from purely technical roles to more strategic, influential positions within organizations.
Essential AI Skills For Modern Technology Professionals
To thrive in this AI-centric landscape, engineers and technology-savvy business professionals should consider cultivating some of the most in-demand skills.
1. Machine Learning And Deep Learning: Gain proficiency in popular frameworks and libraries such as TensorFlow, PyTorch and scikit-learn.
2. Data Science And Analytics: Develop strong skills in statistical analysis, data visualization and big data technologies.
3. AI Ethics And Governance: Understand the ethical implications of AI and ensure responsible, unbiased use of these technologies.
4. Cloud Computing For AI: Master cloud platforms that offer AI and machine learning services, such as AWS, Google Cloud or Azure.
5. Generative AI Tools: ChatGPT generates human-like text, browser tools retrieve real-time information and Synthesia creates AI-generated videos with avatars, all of which can be used for training, marketing and corporate communications.
Navigating The Challenges: Ensuring Ethical AI Use
While the benefits of AI in the tech industry are undeniable, we must also address the significant challenges that come with its implementation. A primary concern that looms large in the minds of responsible professionals is the potential for bias and negative outcomes if AI is not deployed with careful consideration and oversight.
To combat these challenges, a multifaceted approach is necessary. First and foremost, regular audits of AI systems for potential biases are crucial. These audits should be comprehensive, examining not just the output of AI models but also the data they're trained on and the algorithms they use. By systematically reviewing your AI systems, you can identify and address biases before they lead to harmful consequences.
Equally important is the implementation of diverse datasets in the training of AI models. The familiar adage of "garbage in, garbage out" holds especially true in AI. If you train your models on data that reflects only a narrow slice of society, you can't expect them to make fair decisions for everyone. By consciously curating diverse, representative datasets, you can work toward AI systems that are more equitable and inclusive in their decision-making processes.
However, even with the best datasets and most rigorous audits, you cannot rely solely on automated systems for critical decisions. Maintaining human oversight in key decision-making processes is paramount. Human judgment, with its capacity for nuance, empathy and ethical reasoning, serves as a crucial check on AI systems. This human-in-the-loop approach ensures that AI remains a tool to augment human decision making rather than replace it entirely.
AI As A Core Competency
Looking ahead, the integration of AI skills in tech is not just a trend—it's the new standard. As companies continue to invest heavily in AI technologies, the ability to effectively leverage these tools will become a critical differentiator for tech professionals. Those who proactively acquire and hone their AI skills will not only command higher salaries but will also play pivotal roles in shaping its applications across industries.
Embracing The AI-Powered Future Of Tech
The message is clear: AI is reshaping the landscape, creating both unprecedented opportunities and new challenges. Professionals who embrace AI skills are not just securing higher salaries; they're positioning themselves at the forefront of a technological revolution that's transforming industries and societies.
As we navigate this AI-driven future, remember that the goal is not to replace human ingenuity but to augment it. By combining the power of AI with creative problem-solving, critical thinking and domain expertise, we can drive innovation forward in ways we've never seen before.
The future of technology is here, and it's powered by AI. Are you ready to lead the charge?

title: Council Post: The VC Guide To AI’s Transformation Of Traditional Business Services
text:
Victor Orlovski is founder of R136 Ventures, a Silicon Valley-based VC firm focused on scaling mid- and late-stage B2B and fintech startups.
As venture capitalists (VCs), our role extends beyond merely funding startups; we actively help shape the trajectories of emerging technologies and industries. With venture capitalists backing one-fifth of the companies that went public in the U.S. in the 21st century, this impact is profound, even as venture capital represents a modest fraction of the financial markets—less than $1 trillion in active investments compared to over $200 trillion in public and fixed income markets.
Our strategic involvement in technology-driven investments, like those in artificial intelligence, uniquely positions VCs to catalyze and capitalize on the profound disruptions that reshape our economic landscape. My engagement with technology-driven investments has offered me unique insights into the disruptive power of artificial intelligence—a force poised to reshape our economic landscape just as profoundly as any technological revolution before it.
The Inevitable Rise Of Disruption
As the saying goes, every new beginning comes from some other beginning’s end. Innovation naturally leads to disruption, which, at its peak, we recognize as an industrial revolution. From the steam engine initiating the first wave in the early 19th century to the advent of computer chips sparking the third wave in the 1960s, each revolution has dramatically reshaped society. These seismic shifts have halved in emergence time with each wave, underscoring an exponential curve in technological transformation. Yet, for the last 60 years, no new wave has been recognized—until now.
The Fourth Industrial Revolution: AI’s Era
Today, we stand on the brink of the fourth industrial revolution, driven not by a singular invention but by a confluence of advancements in computing power (particularly GPUs), expansive data sets and groundbreaking algorithms like large language models (LLMs). This new infrastructure, though still evolving, is ushering in applications that I believe could redefine our existence just as profoundly as electricity and the internet did.
Transformative Sectors: From Media To Healthcare
AI’s most immediate impact has been on the media sector, transforming how we consume entertainment and news. I believe the shift toward hyper-personalized content, driven by smart algorithms, is just the beginning. AI could further revolutionize content creation, making it more cost-effective and tailored than ever before. For venture capitalists, this represents an opportunity to invest in AI-driven content creation platforms that are redefining media production and distribution. Strategic investments in these platforms could yield significant returns if the demand for customized content continues to grow.
Beyond media, AI is set to overhaul service industries and support functions. Call centers, sales and marketing departments, traditionally reliant on human labor, are ripe for AI-driven automation. This transition could not only reduce costs but also enhance service quality and speed, reducing or eliminating customer wait times and achieving unprecedented service levels. Investing in AI solutions that automate these functions could be a lucrative opportunity for VCs, especially in sectors where customer interaction is a bottleneck.
The Evolution Of Work: AI’s Broader Implications
As AI automates routine tasks, the demand for junior and middle-level programmers will likely wane and be replaced by AI systems that can enhance coding efficiency by 55% or more. Similarly, in fields like healthcare diagnostics and drug discovery, AI’s analytical capabilities may soon outperform human experts. When investing in this area, consider focusing on startups that are pioneering these AI-driven tools, particularly in diagnostics and drug development, as they are poised to disrupt traditional industries dramatically.
Challenges And Risks In AI Investments
While the opportunities in AI-driven transformation are vast, they come with a set of challenges that venture capitalists and entrepreneurs must navigate. Regulatory challenges are at the forefront, as governments worldwide are still formulating policies to manage the ethical implications of AI, such as privacy concerns and data security. This regulatory landscape can significantly slow down progress, as seen with blockchain technology, where regulations often stifle innovation rather than foster it. Technological unpredictability also poses a significant risk, as the rapid pace of AI development can render technologies obsolete quickly, potentially stranding investments in earlier technologies.
The Future Of Employment And Innovation
Despite fears of AI-induced unemployment, history shows that while technological revolutions may displace some jobs, they create more opportunities. While humans are being phased out of roles in the real economy, particularly in digital services such as call centers, customer support, legal and finance, AI is poised to boost the virtual goods economy. The burgeoning AI-driven education sector, for example, has the potential to revolutionize learning and skill development in ways that enable personalized education for people all over the planet.
Moreover, the creator’s economy, powered by AI tools, may help creators build new value in this expanding virtual economy, offering new avenues for creativity and income. Venture capital can play a pivotal role here, funding innovative educational platforms and creator tools that capitalize on these emerging markets.
Venture capital, although a small player in the financial world, often has an outsized impact on innovation. As we navigate this AI-driven landscape, I believe the role of VCs is more important than ever, not just in funding new ventures but in shaping a future where technology enhances human capabilities and opens new frontiers. As we have adapted to past revolutions, so too will we learn to harness the vast potential of AI.

title: Airline Pricing Systems Are ‘Ancient.’ Here’s How AI Can Help
text:
An Israeli company says that airline revenue management systems, first developed in the 1950s, need an update from artificial intelligence.
“When you go to a legacy world like airlines, their infrastructure is ancient,” Fetcherr CEO Roy Cohen said in an interview. The trouble with the legacy revenue management systems is that, in the end, “A human being needs to make a decision” on pricing, he said. But “AI looks at millions of data points and simulates what is the best next action to reach the goal of the airline,” he said.
Typical revenue management has fare levels in buckets. When one bucket is sold out, it moves to the next. “AI supercharges your ability to make decisions” on pricing, rather than just moving to a higher fare when one is sold out, Cohen said.
He said the current array of revenue management systems is “quite a mess” with “no consistency.” Bigger carriers such as Delta have their own revenue management systems, which they update, but smaller carriers either try to keep up or buy from vendors such as Amadeus.
At an investor conference in December, Delta President Glen Hauenstein said the carrier had recently began experimenting with AI for pricing. The technology can help to determine “the amount people are willing to pay for the premium products related to the base fares,” he said, noting that Delta pricing analysts can look at what the technology recommends that the carrier should be charging. “It takes a lot of time and a lot of effort out of the feedback loops, and it really automates, it streamlines and accelerates our ability to move faster,” he said.
While Delta appears to lead peers in using AI for revenue management, it’s clear that various aspects of the airline industry can be enhanced with the newer faster technology.
United Airlines said Tuesday it uses AI in its effort to provide passengers with text messages that include detailed information on the causes of flight delays as well as revised schedules. “Earlier this year, we tapped gen AI to help with these messages,” the carrier said in a prepared statement. “Now, gen AI supports customer messages by reviewing flight data and drafting text updates.
“The addition of gen AI has helped our storytellers increase the number of custom flight updates that gets sent out, so even more flights are receiving more relevant and helpful information,” United said. American did not respond to an email questioning its use of AI.
Additionally, Travelport, a Great Britain-base travel booking company said Wednesday that it recently introduced a tool that uses AI to search billions of trip options from hundreds of airlines. The tool returns search results faster than the average airline search response time in their direct channels said Travelport, which supports agencies and online booking sites.
Fetcherr’s Cohen said that in revenue management, “As a human being makes a decision, we take data points,” But there are so many data points, not just fares and schedules but also “weather and fuel hedging and politics and seasonality.” Conventional revenue management looks primarily at “the velocity of consumer buying.” As an example, a ticket may sell for $200 and demand may push the price up to $275, at which point, “everybody stops buying,” he said.
The Fetcherr model is better able to select a price point between $200 and $275, he said. How does Fetcherr select the price point? “That’s the secret sauce,” he said. “We’ve been training our engine, using all the data we can get our hands on. We are very stealth about how we work. We know we are developing something new.”
Fetcherr said its airline clients include Azul, Royal Air Maroc, Virgin Atlantic, Viva Aerobus and WestJet. The Fetcherr system is “very versatile,” Cohen said. “We can plug it in to almost anything anywhere. We can automate all the manual processes. We can reduce the analysts’ daily procedures by putting all the information in front of them. AI will recommend on every fare what needs to be changed.”
WestJet spokeswoman Madison Kruger said Wednesday that the partnership with Fetcherr “will enable us to leverage AI technology in efforts to streamline and optimize our prices and inventory management, allowing WestJet to enhance guest experience and affordability, in service of our guests and our people.”
Incorporated in 2019, Fetcherr has offices in Netanya, Israel; Miami and Warsaw. Cohen said revenues are in the tens of millions and the company is profitable, but he did not provide specifics. The company said in June that it had raised $90 million, bringing its fundraising total to $111 million.ted

title: SAG-AFTRA’s AI Deal: A $5 Billion Gamble On The Future Of Voice Acting
text:
SAG-AFTRA, the union representing 160,000 actors and media artists, has signed a landmark agreement with AI startup Narrativ, an online marketplace where brands create audio ads using artificial intelligence. This deal has the potential to reshape the multi billion voice acting industry.
Under this agreement, SAG-AFTRA members have the option to license a digital replica of their voice to Narrativ for use in audio advertising. The union and Narrativ have negotiated terms that address informed consent, compensation, and other essential AI-related protections. “Not all members will be interested in the opportunities that licensing their digital voice replicas might offer, and that’s understandable. But for those who do, you now have a safe option,” said SAG-AFTRA National Executive Director & Chief Negotiator Duncan Crabtree-Ireland.
This agreement is promoted as an ethical framework for AI in voice replication. But could it could also accelerate the shift from human to artificial voices, raising critical questions about the future role of human voice in media.
The voice acting market, valued at $4.4 billion in 2019 and projected to reach $5.2 billion by 2027 , now faces a paradigm shift. SAG-AFTRA's deal, while seemingly protective, could paradoxically hasten the industry's AI transition.
Currently, a voice actor might earn $500-$2000 per commercial voiceover. Following the Narrativ deal, the same actor might receive a one-time payment of $5000-$10000 for their voice rights, but see a significant reduction in booking frequency. In the long run, only top-tier actors may retain regular work, with a significant number of audio roles replaced by AI generated voices, reducing work opportunities for many actors.
Industry experts project a potential 30-50% reduction in traditional voice acting jobs within the next decade, as AI-generated voices become more sophisticated and cost-effective. This shift could translate to a $1.5-$2.5 billion market transformation, with funds redirecting from actor salaries to AI companies. The devil is in the detail, has the Union effectively considered the consequences of AI “training’?
The Data Gold Rush
At the heart of this deal lies the value of voice data. One of the most critical and often overlooked aspects of this deal is how it facilitates AI model training. AI systems require vast amounts of high-quality voice data to improve their performance. Once a company has permission to use an actor's voice, they can manipulate and analyze it to train future AI actors, likely without additional compensation to human actors. Each voice licensed to training contributes to the overall improvement of AI voice technology, gradually reducing the need for human actors.
Tech analysts estimate that a comprehensive voice dataset could be worth millions in AI development. For instance, a single actor's voice data, priced at $10,000 today, could contribute to AI models potentially generating hundreds of thousands in revenue over time. Consider an AI company that acquires 100 voice actors' data through this deal. They can use these voices not just for direct replication, but to train their AI to understand the nuances of human speech, emotional inflection, and even regional accents. Over time, this could lead to an AI capable of generating entirely new, realistic voices without any additional human input.
The deal positions voice actors as a temporary cost in the AI companies' long-term strategy. Initially, AI companies hire actors and use their voices, complying with union standards. During this period, they gather invaluable data to improve their AI models. As AI capabilities improve, media companies can begin to reduce their reliance on human actors. A small number of high-profile actors may be retained for public relations purposes. Eventually, companies could have the capability to generate an infinite variety of voices without human input.
The Replacement Of The Replacement
A potential timeline might look like this: In years 1-2, we would see heavy use of licensed actor voices. Years 3-4 would show increased use of AI-generated voices based on actor data. By years 5, the majority of voices could be AI-generated, with only select human actors retained. The voice acting industry may shift from a model based on individual performances to one focused on voice data sales and AI programming.
This situation also presents significant ethical challenges. Does AI replication fundamentally change the nature of voice acting as an art form? Is it ethical for current actors to sell their voices if it potentially harms future generations of voice actors? How can consumers be made aware of when they're hearing an AI voice versus a human?
Legal Minefield and Intellectual Property Concerns
The agreement opens up unprecedented legal challenges. Intellectual property lawyers warn of potential class-action lawsuits over voice rights, with damages potentially reaching hundreds of millions if AI-generated voices are misused or replicated without proper consent. Who owns an AI-generated voice that's based on multiple human voices? How can actors protect themselves from unforeseen or unauthorized uses of their voice data? How will these agreements be enforced across different legal jurisdictions? Who is responsible if an AI-generated voice is used in defamatory or fraudulent content?
This U.S.-centric deal could have far-reaching consequences. International voice-over markets, particularly in Europe and Asia, may face pressure to adopt similar AI-friendly policies, potentially leading to a $1 billion shift in the global market structure within five years. The impact of this deal extends far beyond the U.S. borders. Production companies worldwide may start favoring markets with more AI-friendly regulations. The globalization of voice AI could lead to a homogenization of accents and vocal styles in media.
Alternatives and Potential Solutions
Instead of embracing AI voice replication, alternative approaches could include pushing for laws that limit AI use in voice acting, similar to regulations in other industries threatened by automation. Supporting technological solutions where voice use can be tracked and controlled is another possibility. Exploring models where AI assists human voice actors rather than replaces them could be a middle ground.
The era of the movie star is fading, and the creator economy has emerged as a dominant force, with cartoon voice-over work now leading the industry. For instance, the current number one movie is "Inside Out 2," highlighting the growing success and influence of voice-over talent in today’s entertainment landscape.
In the past, when coal miners faced the threat of technological advancements, they could withhold their labor—a powerful act given the courage and technical skill required to mine. However, in today’s world, where the creator economy thrives and reality shows dominate a post-movie star landscape, the collective power of actors to withhold their labor feels increasingly fleeting. Their influence may now be as disposable as the voice of HAL 9000, a relic of a bygone era, faintly echoing in the rapidly evolving digital age.

title: Council Post: How To Leverage AI To Improve Processes And Boost Credibility

All the content that your company is producing that is unique to the organization can be used to create mini expert systems to enhance customer interactions. Use AI to analyze all your blog posts, and make the content available in an AI application for prospects so they can interact and understand your expertise quickly. This will increase sales and reduce sales cycle times. - Manoj Tandon, Dark Rhino Security
