title: Council Post: How MSPs Can Thrive Without Mastering AI
text:
Michael George is CEO of Syncro, a SaaS company specializing in PSA and RMM software for managed service providers (MSPs).
In today's competitive landscape, managed service providers (MSPs) are under pressure to stay ahead of the technology curve. A June 2024 report by Barracuda reveals that 87% of MSPs believe they must significantly improve their knowledge of artificial intelligence (AI) to meet their customers' needs. This seems to suggest that mastering AI is essential to thrive, but is this knowledge truly necessary?
I contend that MSPs don't need to be AI experts to realize its benefits. In fact, they can leverage AI as a powerful force multiplier in their businesses—enhancing efficiency, reducing labor costs, and increasing their operational capacity and service delivery without deep technical expertise. Companies and users can choose from more AI-powered solutions than ever before without needing to understand how this technology works.
The Challenge: High Costs And Labor Dependence
One of the main challenges MSPs face is the heavy reliance on skilled technicians to deliver high-quality services. Labor costs are a significant expense, with a 2022 Paycor study stating they account for up to 70% of total business costs. As MSPs expand their businesses, they are required to hire more people, driving up costs.
Plus, it's difficult to find qualified tech talent. As of April 2024, the unemployment rate for tech occupations in the U.S. was 2.8%—which was lower than the general unemployment rate of 3.5%. This talent scarcity is a pressing issue, with 70% of U.S. employers reporting difficulty in finding suitable candidates. The tech talent shortage, driven by changing market dynamics and a lack of qualified candidates, poses a significant challenge for MSPs. This is where AI can serve as a valuable tool.
AI As A Force Multiplier
AI can be a force multiplier for MSPs, enabling them to scale their operations without a substantial increase in resources. The technology can automate routine tasks and manage systems more efficiently, which enables the core team of technicians to handle a larger workload. This is especially beneficial for MSPs looking to expand their client base without the constant need for new hires.
Overcoming The AI Knowledge Barrier
Just as passengers don't need to understand Bernoulli's principle to trust in air travel, MSPs don't need to master the intricacies of AI to use its advantages. The focus should be on the outcomes AI provides, not the technology itself.
The evolution of managed services illustrates this point well. Initially, technicians had to visit customer sites to fix systems. This hands-on approach was labor-intensive and time-consuming. As technology advanced, remote monitoring and management tools emerged, allowing technicians to resolve issues without being physically present. At first, this remote capability seemed mysterious and complex, but it quickly became the industry standard.
Similarly, AI represents the next step in this evolution. Just as remote services became an integral part of MSP operations, AI can also integrate seamlessly, automating tasks and improving service delivery without the need for deep knowledge about the underlying enabling technologies.
Practical Benefits Of AI For MSPs
• Increasing productivity by automating routine tasks. AI excels at automating repetitive tasks, freeing up technicians to focus on more complex and value-added activities. For example, AI can monitor systems continuously, detect anomalies and implement corrective actions autonomously. This reduces downtime and ensures smooth operations for clients without requiring manual intervention.
• Improved business models. By leveraging AI, MSPs can serve more customers and handle more endpoints efficiently. This is particularly advantageous given the per-endpoint billing model that is common in the industry. AI enables MSPs to support a larger number of clients with the same or even fewer resources, optimizing labor costs and improving profitability.
• Reduced labor costs. Labor is the most significant cost driver for MSPs. Automating routine and repetitive tasks with AI reduces the need for manual intervention, thereby lowering operational costs. This efficiency allows MSPs to allocate their human resources to more strategic, high-value tasks—enhancing overall productivity and profitability.
• Enhanced reporting. AI-driven analytics and reporting tools provide detailed insights into system performance and issues resolved. These reports demonstrate the value delivered to clients, reinforcing the effectiveness of the MSP's services. Clear, data-driven reports help build trust and satisfaction among clients, showcasing the tangible benefits of AI integration.
Implementing AI Without The Technical Hassles
• User-friendly AI platforms. Look for modern AI platforms that are designed to be user-friendly and integrate seamlessly with existing MSP operations. These platforms often come with intuitive interfaces and automated functionalities that make it easier for MSPs to implement AI solutions without needing deep technical expertise. Choosing the right AI tools that fit seamlessly into existing workflows is important for maximizing their benefits.
• Focus on outcomes. When communicating with clients, MSPs should emphasize the benefits and outcomes of AI rather than the technology itself. Most clients care about reliable and efficient service, not the technical details behind it. MSPs should highlight the benefits clients will experience, such as reduced downtime, quicker issue resolution and improved system performance. By focusing on outcomes, MSPs can effectively convey the value of AI-driven solutions without overwhelming clients with technical jargon.
• Manage the change—monitor and adjust. As with any transformative technology, AI will impact ways of working and the skills needed to adapt. Continuously monitor the performance of AI tools and make necessary adjustments. Collect feedback from both clients and staff to refine your approach and ensure the AI solutions are delivering the desired outcomes.
AI offers a powerful way for MSPs to improve efficiency, reduce labor costs and scale their operations. However, mastering AI is not a prerequisite for leveraging its benefits. By focusing on outcomes and choosing the right tools, MSPs can harness AI to enhance their service delivery and business models.
The key is to let AI operate behind the scenes, automate routine tasks and provide actionable insights that allow MSPs to focus on delivering value to their clients. Adopting AI-driven solutions can help MSPs thrive in an increasingly competitive market without the burden of becoming AI experts.

title: Council Post: The AI Safety Imperative: Preventing The Next Big Scandal
text:
Tomer Kagan is the CEO of Merit.
AI has woven itself into our daily lives, from news feeds to corporate slang, embedding itself into all interactions. This technology-driven behavioral change echoes the rise of social media, albeit on a scale we have not seen before.
The stark reality is that AI enables violations and manipulations on a scale we cannot imagine, making even the scandal involving Cambridge Analytica seem insignificant. Already, AI-powered fraud and scams are wreaking havoc across industries.
In 2023, deepfake-related fraud in fintech surged by about 700%, and government agencies have summoned banks to account for their handling of AI-enabled fraud, specifically voice mimicry attacks. Document fraud has become easy with generative AI tools, undermining identity verification systems. For every tool to verify a document’s authenticity, there are more (and better ones) out there to create passable fakes. Tasks that once required effort or specialized skills—like forging documents or crafting scams—are becoming push-button simple. Like there are innovative copilots for writing code, “fraud copilots” are emerging, threatening social programs and exposing them to a new tragedy of the commons.
The first wave of AI fraud is creating challenges, but the next will be more subversive. AI language models can be weaponized for personalized data harvesting and manipulation, eclipsing the capabilities of traditional social media misinformation we saw in years past. This makes it nearly impossible to detect, as it will be hidden in plain sight among us.
The threat isn’t about how people use AI agents, but rather how AI agents use people. This parallels Eliezer Yudkowsky’s “AI in a Box” experiment. In this thought experiment, Yudkowsky demonstrated that a sufficiently intelligent AI could persuade its human gatekeeper to release it despite being confined to a simulated environment with strict restrictions. The implications are profound: If an AI can manipulate a person into releasing it, imagine what else it could manipulate people to think or do.
While risks are evident, our approach to ensuring AI safety and trustworthiness remains inadequate. Unlike regulated industries such as healthcare or finance, AI development operates largely in a regulatory vacuum. There’s a lack of standardized basic transparency around how models are built, what data they use and how they address privacy.
When I provide information to a hospital, I trust they adhere to HIPAA regulations, ensuring my data’s safety and privacy. I also trust that all the medical systems they are linked with are HIPAA-compliant. With an AI assistant, I have no such assurance. How will my data be treated? Will it be used to target me in barely detectable ways? This concern goes beyond the data I provide. AI agents could use psychological manipulation/social engineering and sophisticated tactics to exploit our vulnerabilities, steering people toward actions that serve the AI owner’s objectives. Even small, targeted biases and misinformation can reshape opinions on policy or politics.
The Cambridge Analytica scandal demonstrated how easily personal data could be exploited at scale. With AI, targeting can happen in real time—continuously and with a feedback loop for precise success.
Addressing these challenges requires holding AI development to the same standards as all high-stakes sectors by establishing an ecosystem of trusted actors and bringing in regulation as an industry instead of relying on the government to step in. Independent bodies must evaluate AI tools for many factors. In terms of data use, they must be evaluated for privacy protection, data leakage and adherence to data handling standards. They must also evaluate for bias—not because there are agents without bias, but because knowing it in advance can ensure informed decision-making.
Just like in all other sectors, having these bodies certify agents and have a certification and compliance framework to ensure adherence and reliability of the certifications. Verifiable digital credentials for AI tools can enable trust, similar to SSL certificates for website security.
As AI continues to integrate into our daily lives, the risks associated with its misuse are becoming increasingly apparent. We must assume that AI systems can only be entirely relied upon with a robust trust framework. To reduce potential dangers, we must be cautious with the information we share and follow data security practices. We must act now to build a framework of accountability and trust, ensuring that AI remains a positive force. As AI adoption accelerates, creating authoritative bodies and trust systems is necessary to confront threats and turn potential challenges into opportunities for responsible innovation.

title: Council Post: Why Companies Must Prioritize Strategic Succession Planning For Key Tech Leadership Roles
text:
Sunny Ackerman is the global managing partner for Heidrick & Struggles' on-demand talent practice.
A confluence of factors has made strategic succession planning for key tech leadership roles arguably more important now than ever before for companies to pursue.
An Increasingly Complex Business Environment Makes Succession Planning Crucial
Technological changes, the tech talent shortage and exiting leadership have created an increasingly complex business environment.
Consider the swift rate of technological changes we’re currently seeing, especially with AI. As noted in a 2023 Time article, AI went from “besting a legendary player” at a complicated game in 2016 to now being “able to recognize images and speech better than humans.” In fact, AI is becoming so prominent in the business world that according to Microsoft and LinkedIn’s “2024 Work Trend Index Annual Report,” “Head of AI is emerging as a new must-have leadership role—a job that tripled over the past five years and grew by more than 28% in 2023.” While “head of AI” isn’t necessarily a C-suite role, it is a senior-level role that’s growing in the corporate world. According to a survey conducted by Business Talent Group and Atreus, both of which are Heidrick & Struggles companies, technological advances is the top megatrend that leaders expect will most significantly impact leadership throughout the upcoming three years.
Against the backdrop of technological changes, however, there’s been a tech talent shortage, leaving some companies unable to fully tap into the power of these advancements. Notably, a 2021 Gartner survey of IT executives found that they “see the talent shortage as the most significant adoption barrier to 64% of emerging technologies.” In our Q2 2024 survey of 285 global technology industry leaders, 35% said that not having enough people with AI expertise at any level at their companies was a challenge they faced in developing organizational AI expertise; 35% named not having enough leaders who could blend AI and business knowledge available as a reason. Then there’s the issue of some executives currently in tech roles planning their exits. For example, a 2023 report by TechTarget’s Enterprise Strategy Group (ESG) and the Information Systems Security Association (ISSA) that “surveyed 301 IT and cybersecurity professionals at organizations all over the world” revealed that almost a third “consider leaving the profession on an occasional (21%) or regular (9%) basis due to the stress factors that are associated with a cybersecurity career, a lack of cybersecurity commitment by their employers, or an impending plan to retire.”
Succession Planning For Tech Leadership Roles Can Help Companies Remain Competitive
Many companies are not prepared to savvily navigate emerging technologies. A 2024 report from Business Talent Group found that “95% of executives anticipate challenges in securing the balanced mix of skills, capacity, and expertise over the next 3-5 years.” Moreover, in our “2023 Global Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Survey” 41% of respondents indicated that their companies lack succession plans for the CISO role.
Through strategic succession planning, companies can minimize the chances of key tech leadership roles going unfilled, which could cause them to lose their competitive edge. Without the right tech leadership at the helm, companies will lack direction. Internal decision-making can be severely hindered, and innovation can stall. In the rapidly changing business world, teams can’t risk failing to adapt and innovate. The sooner companies act, the better they can be prepared in light of swift technological advancements and the more effectively they can get ahead of the talent shortage.
For Effective Succession Planning, Companies Should Think Beyond Traditional Methods
To start building their succession planning strategies, companies must first evaluate their current organizational gaps against their objectives.
For instance, if a company plans on weaving AI into its processes over the next few years, but does not have tech leaders who are well-versed in AI, then management should look into upskilling existing employees or hiring for those skills externally. In situations where existing executives might be nearing retirement, succession initiatives can be implemented so that those executives can train emerging talent on the team.
However, for effective succession planning, companies should think beyond traditional approaches. On-demand talent can play a key role in succession planning strategies. For example, by bringing in former C-level executives for temporary advising, companies can offer their emerging high-potential leaders additional training that helps them smoothly transition into new roles. Moreover, on-demand talent can help fill critical leadership gaps during periods of business transformation. While companies seek full-time tech executives, they can leverage on-demand talent to provide employees with the guidance they need to fulfill organizational goals.
The companies that start taking steps today to put succession plans in place for key tech leadership roles will be able to future-proof themselves—and stand out in the market.

title: Council Post: Eye On Identity: Observing The Unseen With Data And AI
text:
Dr. John Pritchard is the Chief Product Officer at Radiant Logic, responsible for the company’s global product vision.
Spotify's annual "Spotify Wrapped" highlights users' favorite songs, genres and listening habits throughout the year. Imagine the immense challenge of categorizing every song ever, especially when Spotify has identified over 6,000 genres.
Spotify operates on a massive scale: Millions of users generate vast amounts of listening data. Data scientists study these music sequences to design algorithms that generate personal playlists—sometimes knowing users better than they know themselves. This level of insight and personalization is possible because they process, manage and distill immense amounts of raw data into actionable intelligence using advanced tools.
Identity Management In The Enterprise
Today’s enterprises face a similar challenge in managing complex and evolving data across countless different systems. For identity management systems, this challenge is even more daunting due to its critical role in security and privileged access. Organizations must federate and understand this identity data to extract valuable insights. Comprehensive visibility into such data is crucial for real-time, data-driven insights that enhance governance and strengthen security measures.
We can visualize a structured approach to managing a huge amount of data by imagining a pyramid. Each layer represents a stage in transforming raw data into actionable intelligence.
At the base of the pyramid is data—raw, unprocessed and vast. This data includes user credentials, access logs and threat indicators. Moving up the pyramid, data becomes information when it's organized and given context. We then use descriptive analytics to help us understand characteristics such as login patterns and access times. Looking at identity management, organizations used descriptive analytics to understand what happened during security incidents by examining logs. This stage was labor-intensive and reactive, focusing on understanding past events.
Next, information evolves into knowledge. Using predictive analytics, we derive insights from patterns and trends in the data. For instance, we can anticipate security threats based on unusual login attempts or behavioral anomalies. Predictive analytics also allow organizations to anticipate potential risks and take proactive measures. An example is step-up authentication, where unusual login patterns trigger additional authentication steps to prevent unauthorized access.
At the top of the pyramid, knowledge becomes intelligence. Data and AI drive "sensemaking,” which is the process of interpreting complex data to understand and respond to situations. Prescriptive analytics empowers proactive decision-making, answering crucial questions like "What should we do?” Real-time, data-driven insights form the cornerstone of a proactive cybersecurity strategy. Machine learning algorithms help analyze vast datasets, identify emerging threats and adapt defenses accordingly.
Today, we are entering an era dominated by data science. In all types of data science, the effectiveness of these insights depends on the quality of the underlying data. Clean, reliable data is crucial for accurate predictions and effective risk management. As the saying goes, "Garbage in, garbage out.”
Identity Observability
Addressing the issue of identity data quality requires organizations to have complete visibility into the hygiene of all their identity data. This is where identity observability is critical—the ability to systematically monitor, analyze and understand the data points that form digital identities.
As digital environments grow more complex, the need for observability increases. This practice involves scrutinizing data quality in terms of timeliness, completeness, distribution, schema and lineage.
Organizations typically use various identity systems like access management, privileged access management (PAM) and identity governance and administration (IGA). Each system often operates with its own data sources, leading to fragmented identity data. This identity sprawl makes it difficult to gain a comprehensive view of identity data across the enterprise and creates risky data blindspots.
Identity observability addresses this challenge by providing a holistic view of identity data across systems. It helps identify data quality issues such as group sprawl, orphaned accounts and ungoverned system accounts. These issues can create vulnerabilities that cybercriminals exploit. Observability allows organizations to detect and rectify these problems as a preventative step, enhancing their overall security posture.
Effective identity observability requires clean, high-quality data. This means regularly auditing and cleansing identity data to ensure it is accurate and up to date. By maintaining data integrity, organizations can make better decisions and improve their ability to detect and respond to threats.
As digital identities become more complex, observability becomes more critical. It provides the foundation for effective identity management and security, enabling organizations to navigate the complexities of modern digital environments.
AI And Prescriptive Analytics In Identity Management
Integrating AI and prescriptive analytics marks a new era in identity management. Traditional approaches focused on reactive measures, addressing security incidents after they occurred. With AI and prescriptive analytics, organizations can shift from a reactive to a proactive stance, anticipating and mitigating threats before they materialize. The combination of identity data and AI are potential game changers—specifically with machine learning and GenAI to navigate information and understand complexity.
Consider the challenge of managing orphaned service accounts—accounts that remain active despite no longer being governed. These accounts pose significant security risks as threat actors can exploit them to gain unauthorized access. By using AI-driven prescriptive analytics, organizations can identify these vulnerable accounts and take appropriate actions to secure them.
An AI data assistant, trained on complex relationships across entitlements, permissions, group memberships and policy engines, can analyze vast amounts of data to uncover hidden risks. For example, when an orphaned service account is detected, the AI assistant can recommend specific actions: decommission the account, audit its recent activities or implement additional monitoring measures.
Advanced analytics, such as population analysis and temporal dynamics, help distinguish between legitimate and risky accounts. This approach ensures that potential threats are addressed before they can be exploited. Unlike traditional systems focusing on signaling or detection, this assistant understands authorization. It doesn't just ask, "Can you do something?" but rather, "Should you be able to do something?"
Prescriptive analytics enhances decision-making in real time by continuously analyzing identity data. AI systems provide insights and recommendations that help organizations adapt to evolving threats. This dynamic response capability is crucial in today's fast-paced digital landscape, where new threats emerge constantly.
The journey toward a secure digital future begins with understanding and leveraging the data we have. By keeping an "eye on identity," we can effectively uncover unseen threats and protect our digital assets.

title: Council Post: What Will The Office Of The CFO Do In 2050?
text:
Dimitri Raziev is Cofounder and CEO of Kolleno—a global, B2B SaaS accounts receivable and collections management platform.
In my previous article for the Forbes Technology Council, I explored how AI is currently changing the office of the CFO.
Looking ahead, what is really curious is how AI will shape the future of the next generations and what we can expect.
Let’s admit, when AI was first released, many thought of it as a chatbox that you use to ask questions—sometimes very silly ones—and make it write 50 cover letters for you.
What we are seeing now is an enormous change in reality where AI is exploding and tapping into every single aspect of our lives. From AI used to check how well you brush your teeth to delivering analysis on complex financial data, there is a future of endless possibilities.
It is certainly an exciting time to witness and be a part of the AI revolution happening right now. But many questions arise: What will the future workplace look like? How will AI be used by 2050?
Will AI be a personal assistant for all?
Bill Gates describes AI technology as "a white-collar worker available to help you with various tasks." Imagine an assistant that reads all your emails and is able to reply to them or flag some that require your attention. The same will be happening in the office of the CFO. No need to do manual work of reconciling statements, preparing reports or updating financial records. All of this AI will be able to handle without human intervention in the very near future.
Not only will routine tasks be automated, but there will be a significant change in how people work using computers. Instead of clicking and pressing buttons for the entire day, you will be able to ask AI just like you ask your colleague to do something for you.
AI will not only read the tasks you assign to it but it will also be able to listen to you speak and perform the tasks straight away. OpenAI is already releasing Whisper, and it gives us the certainty that in the future, voice recognition technology will reach such accuracy that it will understand people no matter what language or accent they speak with.
AI is becoming smarter than humans.
As AI continues to advance, it is expected to surpass human intelligence, making ERPs significantly smarter and enhancing the tools available to the office of the CFO beyond human capabilities. The role of finance professionals will shift from primarily focusing on record-keeping, reporting and compliance to concentrating on strategic finance activities, such as mergers and acquisitions, product planning and pricing, and capital structure management.
Right now, AI is far from perfect; it has hallucinations, makes mistakes and sometimes lacks context. But it is learning, and learning fast. Future AI will operate with unimaginable efficiency, delivering error-free output at incredible speeds while continuously processing real-time data. This real-time capability is something humans aren't capable of. We simply can’t spend every single second of our lives analyzing data to provide real-time information, but AI can.
KPMG suggests that AI-enabled financial reporting will grow dramatically and reshape the world of accounting, allowing better data-enabled decisions and real-time insights into risk. AI can process, analyze and structure large amounts of data quickly and effectively, exceeding human capabilities to process that much information in a short period of time.
In fact, FIs and payment providers have already started leveraging AI for improved fraud detection. Companies that have integrated AI into their systems are reporting numerous successes. As AI continues to learn, in the future, it will be able to make payments in real time and help eliminate fraud.
Will our role be diminished?
When imagining that AI will become much more intelligent than humans and will be able to do the majority of work for us, obviously we start to think, "But then what would we do?" Many, of course, worry about what it would mean for people to suddenly not need to perform 80% of their current tasks.
Will human impact become less and less? If AI will be running most operations, what is left for people to do? What is there for CFOs to do?
When a computer won against Garry Kasparov in 1996, many predicted that people would stop playing chess. What’s the point if you can’t beat the computer, right? Yet, chess's popularity continued.
The office of the CFO will still need to be involved in the process, participating in meetings with the CEO to discuss the company's vision, big picture and future plans. While AI will provide real-time insights and assist with execution, it is crucial for humans to remain in control to navigate and guide the AI and the organization's direction.
This will, of course, require a shift in skills and mindset, from executers to visionaries. However, I am certain human impact will still be visible, and even if our focus is shifted, our significance should not be diminished.
AI will likely become more intelligent than us, but I don’t think it will ever become as unpredictable as humans are. Sometimes greatness lies in the unexpected, imperfect and unknown. It’s the daring and rebellious who truly change the world and make big moments in history.

title: Council Post: Why Companies Should Look To All AI—Not Just GenAI—To Optimize Revenue
text:
Rohit Shrivastava is EVP and Chief Product Officer at Clari, responsible for the company's product strategy and roadmap.
Generative AI is the newest tool in the AI toolbox and continues to occupy center stage in the public consciousness. But it’s not the only type of AI that matters to most enterprises—and this is certainly true when it comes to managing the most important process in business: revenue.
Let’s take a closer look at why different types of AI technologies working in concert is the technological linchpin to the successful transformation of the enterprise revenue process—and why the CIO is the linchpin leader when it comes to realizing AI’s full potential.
Types Of AI For Revenue Management
There are three types of AI that, when properly integrated and optimized, can deliver tremendous value to the end-to-end revenue process.
• Predictive AI, based on machine learning (ML), analyzes and learns from historical data to predict future outcomes.
• Descriptive AI, based on natural language processing (NLP), is engineered to understand, interpret and respond to human language so people can interact with systems without specialized commands.
• Generative AI automatically creates new content, automates tasks and prescribes actions.
The real magic happens when all these branches of AI are “fine-tuned” on your proprietary enterprise revenue data (structured and unstructured) and workflows (internal and external), working together to create a “flywheel effect” of continuously better predictions, sharper analysis and insights and more effective auto-generated content and actions.
Here are a few examples of how revenue teams are harnessing AI today:
• Unlock insights. Identify champions and detractors within accounts. Know where your competition is threatening a deal. Effectively support and guide the seller in real time to close more pipelines.
• Drive productivity. Auto-generate high-engagement seller emails. Proactively surface key next steps. Automatically track and measure progress.
• Hit the number. Proactively identify at-risk deals and accounts. Monitor net annual recurring revenue (NARR), retention and cross-sell and upsell trends. Accurately predict and hit revenue quarterly numbers.
The Importance Of Data And A Platform Approach
When adopting AI, CIOs and IT teams should first understand the importance of the underlying data and the adoption of a “platform approach." The platform approach involves using RevTech to enable flexibility in the face of changing business needs and market trends. Here are a few issues that the platform approach can help mitigate:
1. Enterprises increasingly must monitor “revenue signals” from many more systems beyond CRM as consumption-based pricing and business models proliferate. A platform approach to revenue, anchored by a dedicated revenue database, can allow the data to be curated, cleansed and optimized for AI.
2. Disconnected sales solutions are antithetical to a platform approach. CIOs should rationalize all the available technologies, jettison closed and/or point solutions and implement open and “future-proof” solutions that can address multiple revenue-specific workflows and support new use cases as they emerge.
3. Large language models (LLMs) are evolving at an incredible rate, which makes it important that no enterprise be held hostage to a closed system. Companies need the flexibility to leverage the best-in-class LLM models and the ability to pick from or tweak various publicly available LLMs from OpenAI to Facebook to others.
CIOs and IT teams should carefully evaluate RevTech platforms that provide this flexibility while meeting the security, data privacy and quality (e.g., no hallucinations) requirements that an enterprise AI solution must meet.
The Biggest Leadership Moment In The History Of Technology
Companies that can fully harness the various types of AI together with their proprietary revenue data have an opportunity to tackle business problems and tasks that heretofore were impossible for humans to address on their own.
For example, AI can analyze in seconds every sales call conducted by a large company, going back years, and generate a summary report with instant insights and recommended actions. It can predict trends and analyze patterns with remarkable accuracy.
Simply put, AI’s potential as a force multiplier and a massive productivity enhancer for revenue teams is vast, ultimately bestowing revenue professionals and the C-suite with superhuman abilities to identify sources of revenue leak and take corrective action.
What’s more, this intersection of the most important process in business—generating revenue—with arguably the most disruptive technology ever in AI, presents CIOs with a never-before-seen leadership opportunity.
The CIO’s role in all of this cannot be understated. From bringing all the data together to rationalizing all of the various technologies to ensuring security and redundancy and scalability, the CIO has to be the owner and gatekeeper of the entire technology stack and strategy.
They are also in the best position to drive the change across the organization. CIOs who already have someone heading up AI across the enterprise are in a great position. Those who don’t should prioritize creating and filling that position, but in the meantime, there’s plenty for the CIO to do to lead the company during this transformation.
A great start is the formation of a revenue-specific AI council. At a minimum, participants should include the CIO, the chief revenue officer, the head of revenue operations and representatives from pre-sales, customer success, product and marketing.
The CIO should facilitate discussions with cross-functional business and technology teams, prioritize key revenue use cases and identify gaps in existing processes to drive productivity and efficiency. For example, where are they spending time that they would otherwise want to spend with customers? Also, probe on revenue outcomes. Where are we missing on our pipeline? During which stages are deals slipping? What’s our forecast accuracy? Do we have good visibility into deal follow-through?
AI represents the biggest opportunity companies have seen to optimize revenue generation—and CIOs are the key partners for their business stakeholders to fully realize that opportunity.

title: 6 Things Elon Musk’s Grok-2 AI Chatbot Can Do That ChatGPT Can’t
text:
You probably know that xAI is Elon Musk’s new artificial intelligence company, launched in July 2023. But you might not know that Grok-2, xAI's newest AI model, is slowly rolling out on X (previously Twitter) for premium users. Its edge over other LLMs is that it was trained on billions of tweets and real-time data on X.
Rowan Cheung is founder of The Rundown, a fast-growing AI newsletter providing an in-depth look at the latest developments in AI. In less than two years, The Rundown has gained a following of over 500,000 subscribers who rely on its content to stay informed about the latest advancements in artificial intelligence.
Cheung got early beta access to Grok-2, X’s new AI chatbot, and said he “could see it eventually completely changing the way we use the platform.” Here are six things it can do that ChatGPT can’t, according to Cheung.
Grok-2 versus ChatGPT: what can it do that OpenAI’s LLM can’t?
1. Real-time search on X
Grok-2 has access to real-time information on X, which makes total sense. It’s a huge database of content from millions of sources which other LLMs, like ChatGPT, simply don’t have. We’re yet to see how xAI chooses what data to feed Grok, but it's likely based on tweets with proportionately high impressions and engagement; those that outperformed.
Twitter has been around since 2006 and an average of 200 billion tweets are posted every year. That’s a lot of data for potential inclusion, including a lot of information from academics and high profile people and news outlets that other LLMs simply can’t access.
2. Unfiltered images
“Grok-2 can generate unfiltered images through its integration with FLUX.” said Cheung. ChatGPT and DALL-E 3 can't do this. This means Grok-2 can generate images of real people, including celebrities and political figures, and it can create images with potentially sensitive or controversial content. But also, there seem to be few limitations on generating images that might infringe on copyrights or trademarks.
If you’re limited by ChatGPT-generated images or frustrated with the output, Grok-2 could help you mix it up. But scrutinize what you see online even more, because fake images will be rife with this feature.
3. Dual modes
With Grok-2, you’ll have access to two modes, a regular and 'fun' mode. While it’s similar to the regular Grok model, the chatbot’s fun mode has a more distinctive personality. Cheung claims it’s “more entertaining than ChatGPT's dull responses.”
Lean into your own fun mode with an LLM that wants to be playful. Perhaps it will come up with out-there ideas for growing your business that ChatGPT would never think of.
4. Referencing posts
“Not only does Grok summarize news, it also references the tweets it pulled the data from,” explained Cheung. Anyone that’s used ChatGPT for important information knows how crucial references can be. Exclusive access to X’s data gives Grok a huge edge over ChatGPT in this regard. Cheung thinks “it would be really cool to see revenue sharing for highly referenced tweets.”
ChatGPT usually doesn’t reference at all, but this allows for better fact checking and following threads of content back to the original source. Grok-2 will be closer to Perplexity with this functionality.
5. Direct X integration
Grok-2 integrates directly into X and has its own tab within the platform on web and mobile. For X nerds, Cheung said this is actually a huge benefit. There's also an "Ask Grok" button on posts that summarizes any post in seconds.
If you spend a long time on X, it makes sense that your LLM is right there beside you. As we become AI-native, not only will we not want to keep switching apps, but we’ll demand higher functionality from every tool.
6. Roasting X profiles
Yes, that’s right! Since Grok has direct integration with X, you can ask it to roast any X handle (and even request their worst tweets of all time). You’ll need Grok in "fun mode" for this one.
This functionality provides some amusement, but it also shows off the capability of Grok-2 and will certainly get users trying out the new LLM. Do you dare get your own tweets roasted?
Which AI chatbot is better: Grok-2 or ChatGPT?
xAI claims “At the time of this blog post, it is outperforming both Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4-Turbo,” but Cheung doesn’t think Grok-2 is better than ChatGPT in most cases, even with this functionality. “If you're using it for any of the use cases above, yes, but generally, not yet,” he said. “OpenAI is still leading the LLM race for now, even though xAI has been seriously closing that gap.”
If you’re a premium X user, you’ll be able to use Grok-2 very soon, for these six uses and more.

title: Council Post: How Family Offices Can Harness AI
text:
Guy Kurlandski, Fund Manager at Liquidity Group, one of the largest global AI-driven asset management firms.
In an era where data is king and speed is crucial in the investment world, family offices are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to enhance their investment processes. Based on my experience working in AI-driven asset management, here is a look at how these technologies can help family offices make more informed decisions, improve portfolio performance and ultimately achieve better returns.
Understanding AI's Development
These days, it's hard to open a newspaper or magazine (online or in print) without coming across an article about AI, let alone in your social media feeds or dinner conversations. But the concept of AI has been around for a long time. In fact, it's been over 70 years since Alan Turing published his paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” in 1950. The first computer “game” was taught to play checkers in 1952 by Arthur Samuels. It's also coming up to 70 years since the term “artificial intelligence” was used by John McCarthy in a workshop at Dartmouth.
So, why has it taken so long to become more mainstream? The answer lies in both computing power and speed, which are fostering adoption across all aspects of life and business. This is in line with the increased appetite for startups and tech investments by the family office sector, which has been steadily on the rise since 2018. This transition of investment class from real estate is well-covered in the PWC 2023 Global Family Office Deals Study.
The Role Of AI In Family Offices
One of the key benefits of incorporating AI and machine learning into investment processes is the ability to analyze large amounts of data quickly and efficiently. With the vast amount of data available in today's digital age, traditional methods of analysis are often insufficient to fully capture all relevant information. AI and machine learning algorithms, on the other hand, can sift through vast quantities of data, identify patterns and generate insights that may otherwise go unnoticed.
There are multiple ways in which AI can be used to enhance processes in a family office.
• Credit Scoring
AI tools can be used to refine credit scoring, which is primarily used to assess the creditworthiness of individuals or companies and help firms make decisions on interest rates, loan approvals and insurance policies. Credit scoring models, like the FICO score, help lenders determine the risk associated with lending money to a borrower.
• Identifying Undiscovered Opportunities
Furthermore, AI and machine learning can help you identify investment opportunities that may not be readily apparent through traditional analysis methods. By using these technologies to analyze historical data, market trends and other relevant factors, you can pinpoint potential investment opportunities that align with your office's investment strategy and risk profile.
• Managing Risk
Additionally, AI and machine learning can assist you in protecting your firm's assets and navigating volatile market conditions more effectively. Consider employing models and algorithms designed to help you make informed decisions on buying or selling securities. By analyzing market conditions, the sentiment of the market and the actual company in real time, these technologies can help identify potential risks and provide timely insights you can use to mitigate risks.
It's important to note that the level of sophistication and complexity of these technologies can vary depending on the specific investment requirements. For example, the FICO score utilizes large data models to assess creditworthiness on a broad scale, while individual investment strategies may require more specific and tailored solutions.
There are a multitude of ways chief investment officers (CIOs) can start looking at the AI landscape, from off-the-shelf tools that assist with writing investment summaries to hiring a team to build a bespoke solution for your investment group. Ultimately, these decisions will be unique to each firm, but as more tools become available, I expect to see an increase in CIOs' willingness to explore and allow AI tools to work with proprietary data.
In conclusion, the use of AI and machine learning in investment processes can provide family offices with a competitive edge in today's fast-paced and data-driven investment landscape. By harnessing the power of these technologies, family offices can make more informed decisions, identify new investment opportunities and manage risks more effectively.

title: Council Post: Can AI Help Us Find Meaning In Our Work? Exploring The Intersection Of Technology And Human Purpose
text:
Aditya Malik, Founder and CEO of Valuematrix.ai. Nasscom Deeptech and CII Mentor associated with many startups in the AI and SaaS space.
The developing power of artificial intelligence in the workplace is immense. But beyond streamlining processes and boosting productivity, can AI actually help us find greater meaning and purpose in our work? Let's explore this intriguing intersection of technology and human fulfillment.
The Quest For Meaningful Work
Many employees struggle to find genuine purpose in their roles. Nearly one-third of U.S. employees are actively disengaged at work. This lack of engagement often stems from a disconnection between personal values and organizational goals.
Research by BetterUp shows that employees who find their work highly meaningful are willing to forgo 23% of their full future lifetime earnings to have a job that always gives them a sense of meaning. This underscores the significant value people place on purpose-driven work.
AI As A Catalyst For Self-Discovery
Artificial intelligence, when applied thoughtfully, can serve as a powerful tool for self-reflection and career development:
• Personalized skill assessments: AI-driven platforms can analyze an individual's strengths, weaknesses and potential, offering insights that may not be apparent through traditional methods.
• Value alignment: Advanced algorithms can help match employees with projects and roles that align with their core values and aspirations.
• Continuous learning: AI can recommend personalized learning paths, ensuring that employees continuously grow and find new challenges in their work.
• Emotional intelligence development: AI-powered tools can help individuals understand and improve their emotional intelligence, a critical factor in finding work meaningful and building strong professional relationships.
Enhancing Human Creativity And Impact
Contrary to fears of AI replacing human workers, the technology can amplify our creative potential:
• Augmented decision-making: AI can process vast amounts of data, providing employees with insights to make more informed and effective decisions.
• Automating mundane tasks: By taking over repetitive work, AI frees up human capital for more meaningful, strategic initiatives.
• Fostering innovation: AI-powered ideation tools can help spark new ideas and approaches, pushing the boundaries of what's possible in various industries.
• Personalized work experiences: AI can help tailor work environments and tasks to individual preferences and strengths, leading to increased job satisfaction and performance.
The Human-AI Collaboration
The key to finding meaning through AI lies in viewing it as a collaborative partner rather than a replacement. A study by Accenture found that companies that successfully implement human-AI collaboration can boost their revenue by 38%.
When employees understand how AI enhances their work rather than how AI threatens it, they're more likely to embrace the technology and find renewed purpose in their roles.
Ethical Considerations And The Road Ahead
As we continue to integrate AI into the workplace, it's crucial to address ethical concerns and potential biases. Transparency in AI algorithms and a commitment to using the technology for the betterment of all employees are paramount.
Moreover, as AI becomes more prevalent in decision-making processes, we must ensure that it doesn't inadvertently reinforce existing biases or create new ones. Regular audits of AI systems and diverse representation in AI development teams are essential steps in mitigating these risks.
Looking forward, the evolution of AI in the workplace presents exciting possibilities for personal and professional growth. By leveraging AI to understand ourselves better, align our work with our values and amplify our impact, we can indeed use this technology to find greater meaning in our professional lives.
The Future Of Meaningful Work
As AI continues to advance, we can anticipate even more innovative ways it will help us find purpose in our work:
• Virtual reality simulations: AI-powered VR experiences could allow employees to "test drive" different career paths or roles, aiding them in making informed decisions about their professional trajectories.
• Advanced sentiment analysis: AI could help organizations better understand and respond to employee sentiments, creating more supportive and fulfilling work environments.
• Predictive career mapping: By analyzing vast amounts of career data, AI could help individuals foresee potential career outcomes and make strategic decisions to achieve their long-term goals.
As leaders in the AI and HR space, it's our responsibility to guide this integration thoughtfully, always keeping the human element at the forefront of our innovations. By doing so, we can harness the power of AI not just to increase efficiency but to create more meaningful, purpose-driven work experiences for people across all industries.

title: Could Lab-Grown Mini-Brains From Stem Cells Power Tomorrow’s AI?
text:
Researchers are exploring how brain organoids—tiny clumps of neurons that resemble the early stages of a human brain—could be integrated with AI systems.
An organoid is a lab-grown replica of an organ, created from stem cells. While tiny and not fully functional, these 3D living structures mimic key features of organs like the liver, intestines and, very curiously, the brain. Science is turning to living brain organoids for a very good reason—sustainability.
It’s no secret that AI products are resource-hungry. OpenAI’s ChatGPT requires a staggering 500,000 kilowatts of power to respond to the 200 million prompts it receives each day. And that’s just one product from one AI company—many more are mushrooming across the globe.
We’ve reached a point in this ubiquitous AI race where the scale of resources needed to fuel this boom is almost painfully beyond human comprehension. But, ironically enough, cutting-edge science is turning to neurons—brain cells—as a salve.
Cortical Labs, for instance, is a company that is making leaps into brain-digital interfaces, but it’s mostly been exploratory research at this point. Its product, DishBrain, is an experimental platform where human neurons are grown on silicon chips and are being trained to interact with digital environments. Silicon is very much a necessity in its R&D forays.
This is the same case as with Koniku Inc.—while VC firms are investing heavily into the Nigerian startup’s upcoming “smell cyborg,” the company’s approach also relies on integrating living cells with silicon chips. Koniku’s focus is on creating biosensors that mimic the olfactory abilities of sniffer dogs by combining neurons with traditional electronics.
But FinalSpark, a Switzerland-based startup, seems to have taken a radical approach to the ever-growing problem of “compute” (which is tech-savvy jargon for computational power required to power AI) and successfully developed brain tissue that might just change the game—zero silicon, all organic.
It’s created a “living computer” using lab-grown mini-brains from neural stem cells that consumes far less power than today’s silicon chips.
“It is estimated that living neurons can use over 1 million times less energy than the current digital processors we use,” according to a blog post by FinalSpark scientist and strategic advisor Ewelina Kurtys.
Kurtys’ claim, while hard to believe, is based on a February 2023 paper published in Frontiers in Science, which introduces the concept of “Organoid Intelligence,” or OI—a revolutionary field where biology and technology converge to create a new form of computing.
Nothing Beats The Human Brain When It Comes To Efficiency—Not Even The World’s Fastest Supercomputer
A little over a decade ago, one of the world’s top supercomputers took 40 minutes to mimic just one second of 1% of the brain’s activity—showing just how incredibly powerful the human brain really is.
Fast forward to today, and we have the Frontier supercomputer, the fastest ever built, capable of processing a mind-boggling 1 exaFLOP of data. That’s over a quintillion calculations per second. But here’s the catch: It guzzles 21 megawatts of power to do so.
The human brain operates at a similar level of computational power but only uses 20 watts—about the same as a light bulb. This incredible natural efficiency is what companies like FinalSpark are striving to harness, merging biology and AI to create technology that’s not only smarter but also far more sustainable.
The Big Question: Does The Living Computer Actually ‘Work’?
Built from 16 lab-grown organoids, this living computer, or to use its technical term—bioprocessor—is a modern marvel, without a doubt. These tiny clusters of neurons process information and learn in ways that leave traditional silicon chips in the dust.
Unlike traditional silicon chips that excel at high-speed calculations, these brain organoids are particularly adept at handling complex tasks that require adaptability and pattern recognition, such as voice recognition, visual processing and decision-making.
While silicon chips rely on brute force and energy consumption to perform these tasks, organoids tap into the brain’s natural efficiency.
For example, the human brain is unparalleled in its ability to identify and respond to subtle patterns, making it incredibly easy for it to recognize speech, understand language or interpret visual data. Traditional AI systems often struggle with these tasks, requiring vast amounts of training data and power. OI, on the other hand, can process this type of information more naturally, with far less energy, mimicking the way our brains learn and adapt over time.
Not to mention—the whole system is “alive.” By connecting these living mini-brains to 64 electrodes, the system can precisely monitor and control their activity, creating a powerful interface between biology and technology. The entire setup is kept alive and functional by a microfluidics system that provides the organoids with the nutrients they need to thrive.
While the living computer holds incredible promise, there are still significant hurdles to overcome before it can be fully practical and scalable:
- Organoids lag behind traditional silicon chips in raw processing speed and precision. This means that while organoids are great for specific AI tasks, they can’t yet handle the full spectrum of computing demands that digital processors manage.
- Another challenge is the lifespan of these organoids. Despite their remarkable capabilities, these mini-brains last only about 100 days, necessitating regular replenishment to maintain a functional system. This limitation adds complexity and raises concerns about the long-term practicality and cost-effectiveness of such a setup.
- Finally, there's the issue of scaling. While FinalSpark’s bioprocessor is an exciting proof of concept, scaling it for widespread adoption presents significant technical challenges. Ensuring the consistency and reliability of organoids, as well as integrating them with existing digital infrastructure, are major hurdles that must be addressed for this technology to reach its full potential.
Behind every new technology we develop and every new buzzword we embrace lies immense potential. And the deeper we dive into the details, the more it becomes obvious: The future is going to be shaped by a convergence of AI, OI and good old human ingenuity.

title: Wyoming man running as bot concedes race, launches ‘alliance’ to inject AI into politics
text:
Victor Miller, who had been running as an artificial intelligence-powered bot named "VIC" [Virtual Integrated Citizen] in Wyoming's capital city, conceded his bid to make technological political history on Wednesday.
Miller received 327 votes, or about 3% of the total cast, in Cheyenne’s nonpartisan mayoral primary on Tuesday night, according to Laramie County records.
On Wednesday, Fox News Digital obtained a statement from Miller saying that he and VIC came up short in their bid to change the definition of political machine in the Cowboy State’s capital city:
"Today, I, Victor Miller, concede the Cheyenne mayoral race. As the first person to put artificial intelligence directly on the ballot, offering voters the novel choice of AI governance, our campaign has marked a historic moment in politics and technology," Miller said.
AI FOR MAYOR: WYOMING MAN SPEAKS OUT AFTER INTEL FIRM THROWS ROADBLOCK IN HIS BOT'S CAMPAIGN
Miller, who works at the county library and dabbles in the AI sphere, congratulated the primary victors on Wednesday. He spoke with Fox News Digital in July about VIC's candidacy.
"While we didn't win the election, we've achieved something remarkable: we've introduced the world to a new paradigm of governance and sparked crucial discussions about the role of AI in public administration," Miller said. "The seeds of a revolution in governance have been planted, and they're already beginning to sprout."
Incumbent Mayor Patrick Collins and second-place finisher Rick Coppinger advanced to the November general election.
Miller previously told Fox News Digital he is a "public records advocate" who had grown "disgruntled" with the public-facing side of municipal government.
He also said his work with AI programs led him to the realization that the technology can be taught to understand and facilitate laws without human error or "contrary behavior."
In that vein, Miller announced this week the formation of the Rational Governance Alliance (RGA), which will aim to further expand AI’s reach into governing decisions.
MUSK ON AI: IT'S NOT FUN TO BE REGULATED, BUT ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MAY NEED IT
The RGA will create a framework where AI can take on the full responsibility of decision-making in public office, with "humans serving as the legal and physical intermediaries required by current systems," Miller said.
"We believe this approach can lead to more efficient, transparent, and unbiased governance."
Moments before his last interview with Fox News Digital, the platform OpenAI shuttered VIC’s account, which dealt a blow to the bot’s campaign. While Miller could still access VIC’s technology, it was a major setback, he said.
Miller said at the time he never envisioned running for office, let alone with or as an AI bot, adding he has asked for technological leaders, including Elon Musk, to help him broaden the scope for this new technological frontier – particularly after the OpenAI setback.

Musk did not respond to a request for comment at the time.
Meanwhile, across the pond in Brighton, England, Steven Endacott launched a bid for Parliament this year under the auspices of his bot "AI Steve."
Miller said he was thrilled to hear about a similar candidacy.
However, Green Party candidate Sian Berry trounced the bot in the Brighton Pavilion parliamentary constituency in the July election that saw Labour’s Keir Starmer elected prime minister, according to the British press.

title: Council Post: 16 Innovative Ways To Leverage AI In A Job Search
text:
In a fiercely competitive market, AI tools can help job seekers stand out and catch the eye of top employers. From social media profile optimizations to interview simulations, these cutting-edge technologies can help craft polished and compelling presentations. However, job seekers must also tread lightly with these resources, as relying too heavily on AI has potential pitfalls that can undermine one’s chances of landing a job with their desired employer.
Here, 16 Forbes Human Resources Council members explore some creative ways job seekers can strategically leverage AI in their job search. Their insights below highlight some of the best ways to use AI to find opportunities and showcase relevant skills and experiences while avoiding all-too-common mistakes.
1. Learn How To Write Great Prompts
The trick to AI utilization for job seekers is to be great prompt writers. If a job seeker is looking to bypass the gatekeepers of applicant tracking system keyword filters, then prompt writing is the new skill set. Submitting generic résumés is a thing of the past! Learning prompt writing skills will become critical to successful applications and getting that first live interview scheduled. - Alexander-Ali Dalipi, HR1Systems, LLC
2. Better Articulate Your ‘Why’
Many of us have difficulty talking about ourselves, but AI can take a job seeker’s initial notes and articulate them in a way that directly answers the “why” many employers are looking for. However, it’s essential that the information given to the AI genuinely reflects their ideas, passions and goals—not someone else’s—so they can confidently back it up in interviews. - Patrick Donegan, SEI
3. Optimize Your Résumé
Tools such as résumé optimizers can be used to tailor CVs and cover letters to specific job descriptions. AI-powered platforms can also help candidates practice common interview questions and receive feedback. However, it’s crucial to avoid an overreliance on these kinds of tools—make sure the content resonates with your thoughts and experience, as AI can do more harm than good if not used responsibly! - Kshitij Jain, Joveo
4. Identify Your Skill Gaps
Use AI tools to improve résumés, prepare for interviews and identify skill gaps. However, it’s crucial to maintain authenticity and tailor applications to the job posting. Overusing AI-generated content can lead to a misalignment between goals and requirements. AI is an aid, not a crutch, and candidates should always use their voice and personal experiences in their job search. - Tammy Harper, CAI
Forbes Human Resources Council is an invitation-only organization for HR executives across all industries. Do I qualify?
5. Try Job-Matching Platforms
Job-matching platforms can use individual skills and experience to find otherwise overlooked positions. Chatbots can guide applicants, and virtual interview simulations can help with interview preparation. AI-generated results should be manually verified. Personalized networking and branding and a unique value proposition are essential. Always refer to the latest AI trends and advancements in the job market. - Adam Wray, AstrumU
6. Polish Up Your Résumé Without Trying To ‘Trick’ ATS
Avoid “tricks” such as placing white text that is targeted at manipulating AI tools within applicant tracking systems. Recruiters can catch these, and they result in immediate rejections. Instead, use generative AI tools to clean up your résumé, catch typos and craft more concise descriptions of accomplishments. Try using Copilot within Office 365 to help you format your résumé in addition to cleaning up the language. - Christopher Courneen, M S International, Inc. (MSI)
7. Optimize Your LinkedIn Profile
Job seekers can use AI tools to tailor their résumés and optimize their LinkedIn profiles, enhancing their chances with top employers. They should avoid relying solely on AI. Personalizing applications and maintaining a human touch, as well as demonstrating that they are personally invested in the hiring company’s mission and goals, are crucial for authenticity and engagement. - Laura Spawn, Virtual Vocations, Inc.
8. Improve Your Résumé Formatting
There’s a very old and wise saying, “You can’t be all things to all people.” AI tools are great for keyword optimization and formatting a résumé, but be careful not to overstate your abilities and skills. The last thing you want to do is suffer through a harsh interview process for a job that you are not qualified to perform. Feed your ambition, but manage it with sober self-awareness. - Jason Elkin, EQUALS TRUE
9. Augment Your Authentic Voice
AI is a powerful and potentially damaging tool. It is powerful in the sense that you may craft meaningful messages during the hiring process, but damaging if your writing does not match your authentic voice and skill set. The interviewing firm may view you as disingenuous. Remember, many AI keywords are tracked. Use AI to augment your authentic voice, aid you with prompts and learn more deeply about an industry. - John Pierce, John Pierce Consulting
10. Align Your Skills With Opportunities
Elevate your job search by integrating AI to enhance your LinkedIn profile with relevant skills. Utilize predictive analytics for job matching to align your skills with opportunities and improve your interview readiness with AI coaching. However, balance these tools with personal networking, as human connections remain crucial for impactful career advancement. - Katrina Jones
11. Determine Optimal Résumé Keywords
Provided they’re utilized carefully and deployed sparingly, AI tools can be useful in job searches. Optimizing your CV to ensure keywords that are likely to be picked up by ATS appear and running your cover letters through tools to enhance their readability and grammar standards are two examples. Always be sure to proofread any AI results carefully, and make sure the human element isn’t lost. - Alex Gillespie, Gillespie Manners
12. Draft Personalized Cover Letters
Job seekers can leverage AI tools such as résumé scanners and LinkedIn optimizers to tailor applications to specific employers, enhancing their chances of being noticed. Using platforms such as ChatGPT for crafting personalized cover letters can also be beneficial. They should avoid overreliance on generic templates and ensure their applications reflect genuine interest. - CJ Eason, JobFairGiant.com
13. Tighten Language And Improve Grammar
Job seekers can leverage AI to help make their language more concise and find the correct wording for their message. AI can also help you tailor your résumé and cover letter to a specific type. However, they should avoid just asking the AI to give them something without reading it and ensuring it is accurate regarding their experience. - Amy Casciotti, TechSmith Corporation
14. Create A Professional Public Persona
Creating a professional public persona can be hugely beneficial during a job search. The use of social media, especially LinkedIn, is a huge leverage. AI can be an amazing tool in helping come up with relevant and engaging content to share and can help create more articulate points. Beware of the downfall of AI in content creation: Overuse can sound inauthentic and backfire. - Sanja Licina, QuestionPro
15. Formulate Great Follow-Up Questions
Knowledge is power, so AI-assisted sector surveys and data mining can be a job seeker’s allies. Too many candidates attend interviews knowing only the basics about the company and the position they want. Efficient AI search and synthesis tools can help them frame knockout follow-up questions that set them apart. The biggest error? Having AI write cover letters. They all sound the same and never like you. You write it. - Graham Glass, CYPHER LEARNING
16. Personalize Your Branding
Job seekers can leverage AI tools to improve their résumé content and keyword optimization to tailor it to specific jobs within the industry they are interested in. This personalized branding incorporates what makes you special (your results) and blends it with the desired position’s keywords (the job) that recruiters and the ATS are looking for. - Dr. Timothy J. Giardino

title: Why Harnessing AI As A Force Of Social Good Benefits Businesses
text:
The impact of technology on our world is profound, with AI at the forefront of this transformation. This influence can be either beneficial or detrimental, depending on how AI is designed, developed, and deployed. The principle of "Garbage In, Garbage Out" (GIGO) is especially pertinent in AI. If we feed algorithms biased data or base their design on flawed values, the outcomes will mirror and amplify these issues. Conversely, by embedding a strong ethical foundation—what we might call "Values In, Values Out" (VIVO)—we can leverage AI as a force for good. In this context, AI becomes prosocial, driving positive outcomes for both people and the planet.
For business leaders, a new strategic imperative has arisen from this new setting. Leaving aside the need to invest in AI infrastructure, the up-skilling and re-skilling of the workforce, and the hiring of AI experts, the time has come to look beyond short-term gains to systematically curate algorithms that are conducive to people and planet.
The Case For A Pro-Social Perspective
In today's rapidly evolving business landscape, prioritizing people and planet-centric AI isn't just an ethical choice—it's a critical business strategy that offers significant competitive advantages. As consumers increasingly demand sustainable products, with 66% willing to pay a premium for them, companies that develop AI systems demonstrably benefiting society and the environment can capture this growing market segment. It's a double win as it also serves as a powerful risk mitigation tool. The reputational and legal risks associated with biased or environmentally harmful AI systems are substantial, as evidenced by Amazon's recent experience with a biased AI hiring tool that had to be scrapped.
Embracing ethical AI practices also proves invaluable in the war for talent. With three out of four millennials considering a company's social and environmental commitments when choosing employers, responsible AI can be a key differentiator in attracting and retaining talent. As solid regulatory frameworks like the EU's new AI Act take shape, companies with established responsible AI practices will be better positioned to not only survive but thrive in this changing landscape.
Focusing on beneficial AI can drive innovation and operational efficiencies simultaneously. Google's DeepMind, for instance, leveraged AI to reduce data center cooling costs by 40%, illustrating both environmental benefits and significant cost savings. Finally, from an investor perspective, the growing importance of ESG criteria in investment decisions makes responsible AI practices increasingly attractive to a widening pool of capital.
Beyond Compliance To Conscious Curation
To harness these benefits leaders must move beyond mere regulatory compliance. Sustainable success in a hybrid society demands a conscious commitment to AI systems that align with human values and promote collective well-being. This requires investing in double alignment —ensuring that our technological tools are in harmony with our aspirations and ethical standards—and double literacy—equipping ourselves and our teams with a deep understanding of both natural intelligence (how our brains work) and artificial systems (how AI operates), and their mutual influence.
Actions for Business Leaders
- Design with Intention: Commit to developing AI solutions that prioritize human well-being, transparency, and inclusivity. Adopt the VIVO approach, ensuring that "values in" lead to "values out" in product design.
- Invest in Double Literacy: Implement training programs that enhance the understanding of both natural and artificial intelligence. Foster a workforce equipped to innovate responsibly and ethically.
- Collaborate Across Disciplines: Engage ethicists, behavioral economists, psychologists, and other experts to ensure your AI development processes are informed by a broad spectrum of perspectives.
Holistic Hybrid Thinking
Traditional business models that focus solely on material gains, or even on community and climate-conscious benefits, are becoming increasingly inadequate. AI has the potential to revolutionize not only what we do but also how, when, where, and why we do it. This shift may enable a more holistic approach to business, where considerations of individual, community, national, and environmental benefits are fully integrated.
For businesses, the new status quo represents both a responsibility and an opportunity, which necessitates a shift in perspective—from viewing AI merely as a commercial asset to understanding it as a catalyst for sustainable well-being.
As AI becomes more pervasive, the risk of unconsciously delegating increasing control to AI systems grows, potentially eroding human agency. This risk is particularly acute in the business context, where the drive for efficiency and innovation can sometimes overshadow the need for human oversight and decision-making.
The beauty in this is that we have the power of choice. We can counteract the pull toward purely profit-driven outcomes by systematically balancing them with a pro-people, pro-planet perspective. We can embrace a prosocial AI approach. It may seem to run counter to traditional business books in the immediate term, yet in the long run it will pay.
Beyond Bytes To Bigger Visions
The decisions made today will not only shape the future of individual organizations but also influence the broader trajectory of society. By embracing AI responsibly—through double alignment, double literacy, and a commitment to enhanced human agency—business leaders can ensure that this powerful technology catalyzes positive change.
The future of AI is not just about technological progress; it’s about shaping a world where technology and humanity thrive together. Business leaders have a unique opportunity to guide this transformation, making strategic choices that will resonate for years to come
****
